Regarding the determination of governing law for arbitration agreements without explicit choice, the Court adopted the "closest and most real connection" test, generally linking it to the underlying contract's governing law. Furthermore, the Supreme Court ruled against appointing an arbitrator for non-parties to a contract under Section 11 and established the maintainability of writ petitions against Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act (MSMED Act) orders if the council acts without jurisdiction or violates natural justice.

The Bombay High Court held that disputes arising from an ancillary agreement, even without an arbitration clause, could be referred to arbitration if the main agreement contains one, and confirmed that bilateral fraud allegations are arbitrable. Conversely, it ruled that disputes concerning the enforcement of mortgage rights are non-arbitrable due to involving rights in rem. The Court also permitted the partial setting aside of an arbitral award, specifically removing personal liability imposed on Designated Partners of an LLP while affirming the award against the LLP itself.

The Delhi High Court, in its rulings, clarified that an exclusive jurisdiction clause in an agreement prevails over subsequent communications merely designating a different arbitration venue, asserting that the designated seat governs jurisdiction. It also declined to re-refer a claim to arbitration under Section 11 when a previous tribunal had already found no evidence to support it, preventing re-agitation of conclusively decided matters. Crucially, the Delhi High Court granted an anti-arbitration injunction in a foreign-seated arbitration, emphasizing its power to intervene in "blatantly vexatious, unconscionable, oppressive" proceedings or those violating public policy, such as an arbitrator's non-disclosure of a conflict of interest.

title: No Forced Possession in Delayed Projects: REAT Jaipur Clarifies Scope of Refund Rights
description:
The Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, Jaipur (REAT), in Satish Sharma v. VVA Developers Pvt. Ltd., has significantly clarified allottees' refund rights under the RERA Act. This pivotal ruling underscores that project delay, non-execution of an Agreement for Sale, and arbitrary unit substitution decisively favor the allottee, even when promoters claim partial project completion.

The case originated from an allottee who booked a unit in 2013 and paid over 10% of the consideration, yet no Agreement for Sale was ever executed. Faced with prolonged delays and subsequent offers of different units after partial project completion, the allottee sought a full refund. The Regulatory Authority initially directed the promoter to either offer possession (with interest adjustment) or provide a refund minus 10% administrative charges if the allottee declined possession.

REAT Jaipur modified this order, unequivocally stating that a promoter's failure to execute an Agreement for Sale (a breach of RERA Sections 13(1) and 13(2)) is a serious statutory violation, which prevents them from imposing contractual deductions like administrative charges. The Tribunal affirmed an allottee's unconditional right to a full refund with interest under Section 18(1) if possession is not delivered within the stipulated timeframe. Crucially, REAT ruled that refund rights are not diminished by partial project completion, belated possession offers, or unilateral substitution of units without the allottee's express consent. Allottees cannot be compelled to accept a unit never originally allotted to them.

Consequently, the REAT directed the promoter to refund the entire deposited amount of ₹6,47,212 with applicable interest, without any deductions, within 45 days. This decision reinforces RERA's core objective to protect homebuyers from promoter non-compliance, strengthening the jurisprudence around remedies for delayed projects and statutory breaches.

title: From Possession to Katha: KRERA Clarifies Developer’s Role in Title Completion
description:
The Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority (KRERA) has issued a landmark ruling, directing a Bengaluru developer to facilitate katha (municipal property tax record) transfer to allottees within 30 days. This judgment, in Somashekar HG & Prakruti M v. Kavitha Ramreddy concerning project "AQUATOWNN", reinforces that post-sale title documentation is an enforceable obligation for promoters under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, not merely a formality.

The dispute arose from buyers' grievance of undue delay in katha mutation, despite an express undertaking in the indemnity bond and sale deed. These contractual documents explicitly stipulated the developer's responsibility to transfer/mutate e-katha within 60 days of sale deed registration. KRERA held that these covenants established a positive duty on the promoter to facilitate the mutation process. The Authority clarified that Section 17(1) of RERA views "title completion" as a trinity encompassing registered conveyance, occupancy certificate, and katha in the allottee's favour.

While mandating specific performance for katha transfer, KRERA rejected the buyers' plea for EMI compensation. The Authority stated that RERA's remedial architecture, though pro-consumer, cannot create liabilities for ancillary financial outgoings absent explicit contractual stipulations. The order thus crystallises three key propositions: an indemnity bond under RERA constitutes an enforceable undertaking, katha facilitation is integral to title completion, and compensation for monetary fallout must be rooted in explicit contractual terms. This ruling aims to standardize katha hand-over mechanisms, reinforcing promoter accountability and guiding both developers and buyers on contractual safeguards and regulatory expectations.

title: My Face, My Voice: The Constitutional, Commercial, And Enforcement Dimensions Of AI-driven IP
description:
The Delhi High Court's interim order in Ranganathan Madhavan v G Filmz Studioz & Ors marks a landmark moment for personality rights, artificial intelligence, and platform liability in India. This ruling decisively reaffirms an individual's sovereign control over the commercial and moral value of their face and voice in the era of synthetic media.

Actor R. Madhavan sued multiple defendants, including platforms like Meta and Google, for unauthorized exploitation of his name, image, likeness, and voice. These personal attributes, asserted as distinctive identifiers and valuable commercial assets, were used in AI-generated deepfakes, morphed pornographic content, and unauthorized merchandise. Platforms were included to facilitate enforcement.

The court established Madhavan's persona as both a proprietary and dignitary interest, rooted in constitutional Articles 19 and 21, performers' moral rights under the Copyright Act, and common law. It protects these rights from unauthorized commercial gain and recognizes that obscene deepfakes infringe upon dignity.

Crucially, the court distinguished AI-generated commercial exploitation from legitimate expressive uses. It ruled that AI-enabled personality cloning for deceptive advertising or pornographic content falls squarely outside fair dealing or free speech protections, considering AI an exacerbating factor in such infringements.

The comprehensive interim relief restrains all identified and unknown infringers from using Madhavan's persona via any technology, including AI. A multi-layered enforcement strategy mandates video platforms to remove content, domain registrars to suspend infringing websites, merchandising platforms to delist products, and social media platforms to effect takedowns and disclose infringer details. This strategy assigns compliance costs to intermediaries and aids in identifying anonymous infringers.

This judgment integrates personality rights as a robust economic interest, akin to a trademark, while firmly linking it to constitutional dignity. It offers a hybrid of property, privacy, and anti-defamation norms, establishing a technologically aware, commercially grounded, and constitutionally infused model for personality rights in India, setting a significant precedent for the digital self.

title: Pending Criminal Case ≠ Passport Denial: Supreme Court on Renewal Rights under the Passports Act
description:
The Supreme Court, in Mahesh Kumar Agarwal v. Union of India, affirmed that pending criminal proceedings do not automatically lead to passport denial, underscoring the right to travel abroad as an intrinsic aspect of Article 21 personal liberty. This ruling clarifies that while the Passports Act, 1967, permits regulation, statutory restrictions must operate within defined legal and constitutional limits.

The appellant, facing multiple criminal cases and a suspended sentence, secured permissions from trial courts for passport renewal, with conditions restricting foreign travel without prior judicial approval. However, the Regional Passport Office refused normal renewal, citing Section 6(2)(f) of the Act and demanding specific court permission for foreign travel for a defined period. This decision was upheld by the High Court, prompting an appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court comprehensively interpreted the Passports Act, harmonizing Section 6(2)(f) (mandating refusal during criminal proceedings) with Section 22, which enables the Central Government to grant exemptions. It emphasized the full effect of Notification GSR 570(E) of 1993, providing a conditional exemption for such persons, subject to court permission and necessary safeguards.

The Court ruled that indefinite denial of passport renewal, particularly when criminal courts have already imposed safeguards to ensure the accused's presence, constitutes a disproportionate restriction under Article 21. It mandated administrative authorities to respect judicial permissions granted by competent courts. This judgment prevents procedural safeguards from becoming permanent disabilities, upholding judicial oversight and constitutional guarantees against rigid application of statutory provisions.

title: IBBI's Hybrid Regime for CIRP Compliance
description:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) has introduced a hybrid regime for Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) compliance through its December 2025 circular. This follows the May 2025 update to CIRP forms and a temporary late fee exemption until December 31, 2025. The new circular operationalizes an OTP-authenticated "Modification Utility" on the IBBI portal, enabling Insolvency Professionals (IPs) to self-correct errors in previously filed forms without resorting to formal amendment routes. Corrections made before a form's statutory due date incur no penalty. However, modifications submitted after the due date are treated as new, delayed submissions, incurring a fee.

Concurrently, the circular reactivates delayed filing levies from January 1, 2026, lifting the earlier suspension. For any form whose due date fell on or before December 31, 2025, but is ultimately submitted (whether original, corrected, or updated) on or after January 1, 2026, IPs must pay ₹500 per form per month of delay, exclusive of GST. This fee is automatically computed and collected electronically. An IP correcting a timely 2025 filing in 2026 will pay this fee, which attaches to the calendar month of the eventual re-upload. This regime combines procedural facilitation with economic deterrence, incentivizing early rectification and ensuring both accuracy and punctuality in CIRP filings.

title: Pre-Agreed Online Dispute Resolution Clause Prevails – Amit Chaurasia v. ICICI Bank Limited
description:
The Bombay High Court, in Amit Chaurasia v. ICICI Bank Limited (December 2025), strongly affirmed party autonomy in online dispute resolution (ODR) arbitration while also encouraging consensual settlement. The case involved a borrower challenging a credit facility's ODR clause, which specified dispute resolution through the bank's Online Dispute Resolution Agency (ODRA) via a two-step process: mandatory conciliation followed by arbitration.

The petitioner argued that there was no consensus on the arbitrator's identity and that the ODRA lacked statutory independence. However, the Court held that the petitioner's acceptance of the facility after receiving notice of the web-linked terms and conditions, coupled with a failure to object to ODRA intimations, constituted implied acceptance under Section 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. It further clarified that a pre-named institutional arbitrator, chosen contractually by parties, is not inherently biased or indicative of a lack of consent.

Despite rejecting the challenge to the arbitration agreement, the Court, recognizing the modest monetary stakes and both parties' openness to settle, exercised its inherent powers to direct them to mediation. This ruling sends a clear message: courts will uphold commercial contracts incorporating institutionalized dispute resolution mechanisms, yet simultaneously facilitate negotiated resolutions when parties are amenable, demonstrating that party autonomy and access to justice can coexist effectively.

title: Arbitral Tribunal Alone Decides Who May Invoke Arbitration, Supreme Court Reiterates
description:
The Supreme Court dismissed appeals, reaffirming the arbitral tribunal's authority to decide substantive questions like whether a single consortium member may invoke arbitration. The Court held such questions fall under Section 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, limiting judicial scrutiny under Section 11(6) to merely confirming the prima facie existence of an arbitration agreement.

The case stemmed from an APGENCO EPC tender, where Tecpro, a consortium member, unilaterally invoked arbitration after entering Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). Appellants APGENCO and VA Tech argued the arbitration agreement mandated collective invocation, citing Tecpro's insolvency and leadership change. Tecpro countered that the consortium wasn't a juristic person and its agreement allowed individual representation upon insolvency.

The Supreme Court underscored the policy of minimal judicial intervention, clarifying that the appellants conflated the "existence" of an arbitration agreement with Tecpro's "entitlement" or "capacity" to invoke it individually. Substantive issues, including consortium survival, consent requirements, and liquidation impact, are exclusively for the arbitral tribunal. The Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's tribunal appointment and remitting all substantive objections to the arbitrator under Section 16, reinforcing the principle of kompetenz-kompetenz.

title: Centralising Religious Dietary Certifications: An Analysis of the Food Safety and Standards (Amendment) Bill, 2025
description:
The Food Safety and Standards (Amendment) Bill, 2025 represents a pivotal shift in India's regulation of faith-based dietary certifications, particularly Halal. Addressing long-standing concerns regarding a lack of legal oversight, inconsistent standards, and unchecked private certification practices, the Bill seeks to bring these under a statutory, government-controlled framework.

The legislation expands the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)'s mandate, empowering it to regulate, grant, and monitor religious dietary certifications exclusively through government-notified agencies under the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Crucially, the Bill prohibits private organizations, trusts, or societies from issuing Halal certifications or collecting associated fees, centralizing this authority with designated government agencies and directing all fees to the Consolidated Fund of India. The scope of such certifications is strictly limited to food products for human consumption, with stringent penalties for contravention.

A dedicated Committee on Certification of Religious Dietary Food Items is established to formulate and periodically update uniform national standards for all forms of religious dietary certifications, encompassing Halal, Kosher, and Jhatka. This committee ensures a balanced approach incorporating scientific expertise and inter-ministerial coordination, covering aspects like slaughter, processing, packaging, and labelling. The overarching intent is to enhance consumer confidence, ensure transparency, and uphold accountability within India's food safety regime by balancing respect for religious practices with public health and regulatory integrity.

title: Arbitration At The Guillotine: Inside The Supreme Court’s 269 Page Judgement, UNCITRAL’s Evolution, SIAC-LCIA-HKIAC Perspectives, And The Road To The Arbitration And Conciliation Bill, 2024
description:
The Supreme Court's judgment in Harshbir Singh Pannu v. Jaswinder Singh critically examines how "termination of arbitral proceedings" has been weaponized in India. The Court's deep dive, tracing from the UNCITRAL Model Law to international institutional rules (SIAC, LCIA, HKIAC), reveals how India's fragmented statutory provisions in Sections 25, 30, 32, and 38 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, undermine the arbitral process.

The case, stemming from a hospital partnership dispute, highlighted how fee recalibrations post-counterclaim, and subsequent termination orders under Section 38 for non-payment, can act as a "procedural guillotine," effectively extinguishing valid claims without a merits adjudication. Unlike the clear, consolidated termination frameworks of international institutions, India's Act creates a fog of uncertainty regarding the tribunal's mandate and parties' recourse, diverging from UNCITRAL's intent for carefully delimited termination scenarios.

Recognizing these systemic flaws, the Supreme Court, while partially vindicating the appellant, provided "meaningful suggestions" for legislative reform. The article argues the forthcoming Arbitration and Conciliation Bill, 2024, must: consolidate termination grounds into a single, comprehensive provision; establish a transparent, "terms of reference"-driven fee and deposit regime; and create an express statutory remedy against capricious termination orders.

These reforms, supported by similar critiques in ASF Buildtech (jurisdiction) and Gayatri Balasamy (post-award control), are crucial to transform termination from a weapon into a calibrated safeguard. The Bill's success in translating these lessons will determine whether Indian arbitration achieves parity with leading global forums.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2025
description:
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act) 2025, whose rules were notified on November 13, 2025, establishes a comprehensive framework for governing how organizations in India collect, use, store, and process the personal data of individuals, referred to as Data Principals. This legislation is crucial for enhancing data protection and privacy standards across the nation.

The implementation of the DPDP Act is structured in phases. Following its notification as the effective date, subsequent stages will introduce the Consent Manager Ecosystem in Phase 2, culminating in full compliance and enforcement during Phase 3. To facilitate a smooth transition, the government has provided an 18-month lead time for most of the Act's provisions. The Act also specifies penalties for instances of non-compliance, reinforcing its commitment to robust data privacy.

title: RERA’s Iron Grip Strengthened: Courts Redefine Allottee Rights in Mortgages, Leases & Insolvency
description:
The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA), enacted to safeguard homebuyers, has seen its authority significantly fortified by recent judicial interventions. These rulings have consistently prioritized allottee rights, challenging contractual loopholes and traditional financial claims.

Initially, developers attempted to bypass RERA by structuring transactions as long-term "leases" (e.g., 999 years) rather than sales, claiming their customers were merely "lessees" outside RERA's purview. In Lavasa Corporation Ltd. vs. Jitendra Jagdish Tulsiani, courts applied the "substance over form" principle. They ruled that such agreements, involving substantial upfront "premiums" and minimal "rent," were essentially sales, thereby confirming buyers as "allottees" under RERA and closing this potential loophole.

A more profound challenge emerged from the conflict between homebuyers and banks. Banks, as "secured creditors" under the SARFAESI Act, would seize projects upon developer default, often leaving allottees who had paid for their units with no recourse. The Supreme Court, in Union Bank of India vs. Rajasthan RERA, delivered a landmark decision. It held that when a bank takes control of a RERA-registered project, it becomes a "statutory assignee" and therefore a "promoter" under RERA, assuming the original developer's liabilities to allottees. This decision effectively elevated RERA-secured homebuyer rights above SARFAESI-secured lenders' recovery rights, compelling banks to become de facto monitors of project compliance.

Further strengthening allottee protection, the judiciary addressed conflicts with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). In Vishal Chelani v. Debashis Nanda, the Supreme Court rejected attempts to "hyper-classify" allottees, ensuring those seeking RERA refunds maintained their status as "financial creditors" under the IBC with equal priority. The Mansi Brar Fernandes v. Shubha Sharma ruling clarified that IBC protections are for "genuine homebuyers" seeking shelter, not speculative investors using assured return schemes. Crucially, this judgment also elevated the right to housing to a "fundamental right" derived from Article 21 of the Constitution, providing a robust constitutional foundation for allottee protection and advocating for "project-by-project" insolvency.

These judicial interventions have profoundly redefined the homebuyer's status, transforming them from a mere contractual party to a beneficiary of a constitutionally protected "fundamental right" and a robust "financial creditor" in insolvency. This shift has imposed significant accountability on developers and financial institutions, fostering a more transparent and allottee-centric real estate ecosystem.

title: Madras High Court Partially Sets Aside Arbitral Award for Exceeding Jurisdiction in Applying ‘Alter Ego’ Doctrine
description:
The Madras High Court, in Sugesan Transport Pvt. Ltd. v. E.C. Bose & Company Pvt. Ltd., significantly clarified the limits of an arbitral tribunal's jurisdiction, particularly regarding the doctrines of lifting the corporate veil and alter ego, and the assessment of damages. The Court reaffirmed that arbitral awards must strictly adhere to the contractual framework and cannot extend obligations beyond the arbitration agreement.

The dispute arose from a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) where Sugesan Transport advanced ₹2.50 crores to E.C. Bose for a performance bank guarantee. E.C. Bose failed to repay the amount. During arbitration, E.C. Bose counter-claimed ₹75 crores, alleging a joint venture for a KOPT contract and Sugesan's failure to supply equipment. The Arbitrator partially accepted both claims, directing repayment of ₹2.50 crores to Sugesan but also awarding ₹6.51 crores as damages to E.C. Bose, imputing equipment supply obligations to Sugesan based on documents signed by a third entity (Collate Consultants Pvt. Ltd.) and applying the ‘alter ego’ doctrine.

The High Court held that an arbitral tribunal is a creature of contract and cannot extend liability to non-signatories or pierce the corporate veil; these powers are exclusive to courts. It found the Arbitrator's reliance on Collate Consultants' documents to impose obligations on Sugesan without jurisdiction. The Court further noted that the NCLAT and Supreme Court had already ruled the MoU was a standalone financial transaction, independent of any equipment supply obligations. Regarding damages, the Court stressed that under Sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act, damages must be proven with actual loss and evidentiary basis, not speculative assumptions like the mere encashment of a bank guarantee.

Consequently, the High Court partially set aside the arbitral award. It upheld the direction for E.C. Bose to repay ₹2.50 crores to Sugesan Transport but entirely eliminated the counter-claim award of ₹6.51 crores in favour of E.C. Bose, deeming it unsustainable. This judgment reinforces that arbitral tribunals must operate strictly within the arbitration agreement's contours, cannot apply doctrines like 'alter ego' to non-signatories, and damages must be strictly proven.

title: The Right To A Livable Planet: The Intersection Of Vegan Rights, Human Dignity, And Environmental Justice
description:
Veganism is increasingly recognized as a fundamental human and consumer right, encompassing ethical, religious, and health-based dietary choices, protected under constitutional freedoms. This was powerfully affirmed in a 2025 Bengaluru consumer protection case where Rs. 1,05,146 (plus interest) was awarded to Nisha G., a vegan woman who received prawns in her "vegan" sandwich order via Swiggy from Paris Panini. The incident caused profound emotional distress and spiritual trauma, underscoring the serious implications of violating faith-based dietary restrictions. The Bengaluru Urban District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission found both Swiggy and Paris Panini jointly liable for negligence.

Beyond individual convictions, veganism plays a critical role in combating climate change and promoting global sustainability. Extensive research indicates that plant-based diets significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions, land use, water consumption, and pollution compared to omnivorous diets. Thus, safeguarding vegan dietary rights aligns ethical consumption with vital planetary health goals, highlighting a crucial intersection of justice, health, and environmental welfare.

This legal recognition of veganism not only protects consumer dignity and prevents discrimination but also holds businesses accountable for accurate food representation and empowers individuals to make climate-conscious choices. The ruling sends a clear message about upholding faith, ethical rights, and environmental commitments, emphasizing that evolving legal frameworks must support choices that safeguard both the planet and personal conviction for a sustainable and compassionate future.

title: Defining Financial Debt: NCLT Judgment Confirms IBC Cannot Be Invoked for Recovery of Profit-Linked Investments
description:
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), New Delhi, dismissed a Section 7 application by Modern Solar Private Limited against Claro Energy Private Limited, ruling that the ₹20 lakh advanced was an investment in a profit-sharing venture, not a loan. This landmark judgment emphasizes that these funds lacked the essential "time value of money" component, crucial for qualifying as "financial debt" under Section 5(8) of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code (IBC). Consequently, the IBC cannot be invoked to recover profit-linked investments or to convert failed commercial arrangements into insolvency proceedings.

The dispute stemmed from Modern Solar's advancement of funds for a project, which it later claimed was a loan, while Claro Energy asserted it was a profit-sharing investment. The NCLT's analysis of email correspondence confirmed the original intent was an investment, and subsequent loan restructuring discussions were inconclusive. The Tribunal found no contractual basis for an 18% interest rate, thus failing to establish the "time value of money." It also relied on judicial precedents like Jagbasera Infratech Pvt. Ltd. v. Rawal Variety Construction Ltd., which similarly held that investments in joint ventures or profit-sharing projects do not constitute "financial debt."

The Tribunal's decision reinforces the strict definition of "financial debt" and safeguards the IBC's integrity. It ensures the Code serves its intended purpose as an insolvency resolution mechanism, rather than being misused as a general debt recovery platform for business investments that carry inherent commercial risks, preventing retrospective conversion of such risks into fictional loans to invoke insolvency proceedings.

title: Code on Social Security 2020 Becomes Operational: ESIC Expands ‘Dependant’ and ‘Family’ Benefits
description:
Following the Ministry of Labour & Employment's notification, the Code on Social Security, 2020 (CoSS) became operational on November 21, 2025. Promptly, the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) issued Circular No. N-11011/2/2025-BFT-II on November 28, 2025, directing its disbursing and medical offices to implement the enlarged social security benefits basket.

The CoSS significantly redefines key terms. Section 2(24)(c) expands "dependant" to include widowers and grand-parents, while Section 2(33)(e) brings a woman employee’s father-in-law and mother-in-law within the expression “family.” These are self-executing statutory mandates, obliging ESIC to recalibrate all sanction orders with prospective effect from November 21, 2025.

Operationally, this means a widower-husband can now claim survivors' pension, and maternal or paternal grand-parents wholly dependent on an insured person become legitimate claimants. On the medical front, in-laws of a woman employee are now entitled to outpatient, inpatient, and specialist care under the ESI scheme, resolving long-standing issues regarding family definitions.

ESIC has mandated immediate compliance without any transition period. Field offices must re-examine claims pending on or after November 21, 2025, under the new definitions, ensuring sanction within statutory timelines. Failure to apply the CoSS definitions could expose the Corporation to legal action for delayed benefits. This swift operationalization underscores CoSS as an active charter, extending tangible relief to previously overlooked beneficiaries and reducing reliance on judicial intervention for recognition.

title: FSSAI Crack-Down on Auramine-Laced Roasted Chana: Industrial Dye in Food Meets Statutory Enforcement
description:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued an emergency directive (Order RCD-15001/16/2025-Regulatory) to combat the illicit use of Auramine-O in roasted chana and similar cereal-based snacks. This industrial dye, typically reserved for leather and textiles, is applied to mimic a golden hue but is not a permitted food additive. Its presence renders food "unsafe" under Section 3(1)(zz)(v) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, triggering mandatory enforcement.

Invoking its emergency steering power under Section 16(5), FSSAI mandates a pan-India crackdown across all Food Business Operators, from organized manufacturers to street vendors and e-commerce platforms. State and Union Territory food safety commissioners are instructed to conduct surprise inspections, draw samples, and send them exclusively to a specified panel of four NABL-accredited laboratories validated for Auramine estimation in processed cereals. Detection will initiate adjudication proceedings, with consolidated action reports detailing test results and penalties due within fifteen calendar days.

Violators face severe consequences, including immediate seizure and destruction of suspect stock, financial penalties, and for repeat offenders, imprisonment up to seven years and corporate prosecution, alongside potential indefinite licence suspension. This decisive action underscores FSSAI's unwavering commitment to eliminating industrial chemicals from the nation's food supply, ensuring that food's golden glow derives from natural processes, not hazardous dyes.

title: The Sovereign’s Gate: A Comprehensive Guide to India’s Visa Regime and OCI Framework (2025)
description:
India's immigration framework, governed by the 2025 Immigration and Foreigners Act, meticulously regulates entry as a "profound legal event," balancing individual liberty and state sovereignty. Navigating this complex system requires precision and adherence to specific visa categories and protocols.

The 2025 visa architecture prioritizes e-Visas for convenience. The e-Tourist Visa, for 166+ countries, covers recreation but has strict "Continuous Stay" limits; overstaying leads to severe penalties. The e-Business Visa permits commercial activities, strictly prohibiting employment. Other e-Visas include Medical and Conference types. A significant 2025 update is the mandatory e-Arrival Card, a digital health/itinerary declaration required 72 hours pre-boarding. For specific restricted purposes, the traditional Regular (Paper) Visa with physical submission and rigorous scrutiny is still necessary.

Nations like Pakistan and China are "Prior Reference Category" (PRC) countries, requiring direct vetting by the Ministry of Home Affairs due to foreign policy. India offers purpose-specific visas (Employment, Journalist, Student, Film); applying for the incorrect category is a common error leading to rejection.

The Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Card is a vital framework for the Indian diaspora, granting life-long visa status but not dual citizenship. Eligibility is ancestral (applicant, parents, or grandparents being Indian citizens post-1950), with a strict exclusion for those with Pakistani or Bangladeshi past citizenship. OCI holders enjoy parity with resident citizens in most economic/financial matters but cannot vote, hold constitutional posts, or acquire agricultural land. Documentation requires strict adherence to format; former Indian citizens must provide a Surrender Certificate. OCI re-issuance rules were relaxed in 2025, removing the requirement with every passport renewal.

Common pitfalls include misrepresenting intent (e.g., business on a tourist visa), failing to disclose criminal records, concealing Pakistani origin, or submitting poor-quality documents. Transparent and accurate declarations, alongside meticulous digital hygiene, are paramount. Ultimately, India's immigration laws act as a filter for intent, legality, and security, welcoming those who respect its sovereign rules.

title: Police Power versus Food Safety Officer Jurisdiction : Rajasthan High Court Clears the Air in Ravi v. State of Rajasthan
description:
The Rajasthan High Court, in Ravi v. State of Rajasthan, quashed an FIR and criminal proceedings involving food adulteration and misbranding under Sections 272, 273, and 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) read with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA). The ruling re-established the primacy of the FSSA as a special law over general IPC provisions for identical conduct, emphasizing that once conduct is punishable under the more stringent FSSA, the general provisions of the IPC must yield.

The petitioner argued that the FSSA, being a self-contained code with an "over-riding effect" under Section 89, supersedes IPC Sections 272 and 273 once an offence under FSSA Section 59 is made out. Furthermore, it was contended that only a qualified Food Safety Officer is authorized to investigate adulteration cases, not the police. The charge of cheating (IPC Section 420) was also contested due to the absence of allegations regarding inducement or wrongful loss to any purchaser. The State, conversely, argued that IPC offences retain independent identity and police are competent to investigate cognizable offences like IPC 420.

Citing Supreme Court precedents (Ram Nath v. State of U.P. and Sushil Kumar Gupta v. State of West Bengal), the High Court affirmed that the FSSA, with its comprehensive and often more stringent provisions, overrides general IPC sections 272 and 273, thereby barring simultaneous prosecution. The court found no foundational facts for cheating under IPC 420 in the FIR, dismissing the charge. Crucially, it held that police investigation into adulteration contravenes the FSSA statutory scheme, which vests such powers exclusively in Food Safety Officers. Consequently, all proceedings from the FIR were quashed, though the competent food authority remains free to pursue remedies solely under the FSSA. This judgment reinforces that specific statutory codes with built-in safeguards take precedence over general criminal law for the same set of facts.

title: Restoring Dignity and Property: SC Rules on Mahr and Marriage Gifts
description:
The Supreme Court, in `Rousanara Begum v. S.K. Salahuddin`, has decisively reaffirmed a divorced Muslim woman’s non-negotiable economic rights. This landmark decision ensures her entitlement to property, money, and jewellery received at marriage, aligning with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986. The ruling prioritizes securing dignity, equality, and financial protection, moving beyond technicalities to address women's vulnerabilities post-divorce.

The Court clarified that a woman's ownership rights over such assets persist even after marriage ends. These gifts often serve as a woman's sole financial resource, offering critical economic security and personal dignity. The judgment reinforces Section 3 of the 1986 Act, interpreting it as social justice legislation grounded in constitutional values of equality, dignity, and autonomy (Article 21). It challenges patriarchal assumptions that absorb a woman's property into the marital household, protecting her from post-divorce vulnerability.

The ruling emphasizes that legal interpretation must consider social realities and legislative intent, ensuring women's claims are not dismissed due to minor inconsistencies. It clarifies that the 1986 Act covers assets received "before or at the time of marriage or after her marriage," aligning with Daniel Latifi principles for long-term financial stability. The Court instructs lower courts to adopt interpretations favoring women's empowerment and dignity. Ultimately, the decision reframes women as rights-bearing individuals with enforceable claims to property, reinforcing that a woman's property remains her own before, during, and after divorce. The SC overturned the High Court, directing the respondent to return assets with interest.

title: Behaviour-Based Safety: The Leadership Strategy India Needs to Prevent Industrial Accidents
description:
India confronts a disturbing rise in industrial accidents, despite modern equipment and regulatory frameworks like the OSH Code 2020, which often foster administrative compliance over genuine safety leadership. The article underscores that true safety is a lived culture, not merely a presented metric, illustrated by an executive's silent gesture conveying, "Safety is not something you present, it’s something you live."

Behaviour-Based Safety (BBS) is posited as the critical strategy to transform safety from a compliance exercise into a core leadership value and shared organizational habit. Inspired by DuPont's pioneering 1960s BBS program, which evolved from over a century of safety commitment, the author shares personal success implementing BBS in India. BBS moves beyond rules and checklists to foster a robust safety culture.

While effective BBS implementation requires thorough understanding, as many companies prematurely abandon efforts, it yields significant benefits. Tangible improvements manifest in production, quality, delivery, sustainability, and morale within 10-15 months. Intangible gains include a vibrant culture, increased employee ownership, teamwork, and a harmonious workplace.

Ultimately, safety is presented as a fundamental leadership mindset. Leaders' visible commitment—demonstrated through curiosity on the shop floor, appreciation of safe behavior, and coaching—builds an "invisible shield" protecting people and assets. This shift from prescribed rules to lived practice, where leaders' actions shape belief, cultivates a culture of excellence, trust, and pride, making safety synonymous with effective leadership.

title: Punjab & Haryana High Court Reaffirms Statutory Grace Period for Expired Driving Licences: Insurer Denied Recovery Rights
description:
The Punjab and Haryana High Court has reiterated that a formally expired driving license remains legally effective for the 30-day statutory grace period stipulated under Section 14(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. This judgment, delivered on November 21, 2025, dismissed an appeal by National Insurance Company Limited, denying the insurer any right to recover compensation it had paid to accident victims.

The dispute arose from an accident where the driver's license had expired on June 4, 2001, and the accident occurred on July 4, 2001, with renewal only on August 6, 2001. The insurer argued the driver was unlicensed, constituting a policy breach and entitling them to recovery. However, the vehicle owner contended that the accident, which happened at 10:45 a.m. on July 4, 2001, fell squarely within the 30-day grace period, which commenced on June 5, 2001, and expired at midnight on July 4, 2001.

Justice Virinder Aggarwal, examining the provision's plain language, affirmed that the legislature explicitly defers the cessation of an expired license by thirty days. Citing precedents like State of Haryana & Anr. v. Karkor & Ors. and Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Smt. Santosh Kumari, the Court concluded that the driver was legally licensed at the time of the accident. Consequently, no breach of policy conditions occurred, and the insurer's plea for recovery was dismissed, affirming the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal's original award. This ruling emphasizes that the 30-day extension is a substantive continuation of license validity, necessitating insurers to factor this legislated continuum into their risk assessments.

title: CG-RERA Circular 139/2025: “Notarised” Contract Term Variations and the Sole Collection Account
description:
Chhattisgarh Real Estate Regulatory Authority (CG-RERA), through Circular No. 139 dated November 14, 2025, has translated Supreme Court's disapproval of opaque builder-buyer paperwork into practical directives. These immediate, transversal instructions apply to all project documentation and are framed as conditions precedent for lawful execution and registration.

The circular introduces a "notarisation" protocol: any clause or deviation from the statutory Agreement for Sale (AFS) template (Rule 9's Annexure-A) must be "notarised" by the competent Revenue Authority before execution. This compulsory step ensures that additional covenants (e.g., penal interest, construction milestones, amenities promises) or bespoke riders, whether pre- or post-registration, are publicly attested. This closes the loophole of promoters later inserting supplementary sheets. Non-compliance will lead to penalties, including refusal or revocation of project registration.

Parallel to this, the circular mandates that only the RERA Collection Account number must be displayed across all project documentation—including sale deeds, allotment letters, brochures, and website banners. Any reference to alternative bank accounts (escrow, partnership, or group company accounts) is strictly prohibited. This aims to funnel all payments into the Authority’s dashboard-integrated account, permitting real-time reconciliation and enhancing transparency. Promoters marketing inventory must purge alternative account numbers within seven days.

By making every deviation publicly attested and every monetary destination uniquely identifiable, Circular 139 converts the AFS into a tightly scripted instrument. This directive serves as both a compliance accelerator for promoters and a consumer shield, giving practical teeth to RERA's promise of transparency and protection.

title: Don’t Sell Me This Pen: RBI Prohibits Lending Service Providers From Playing Salesmen
description:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued comprehensive Digital Lending (DL) Directions, 2025 (effective May 8, 2025), to mitigate severe consumer protection risks like opaque pricing, aggressive collection, and data misuse in India's growing digital lending sector.

A central reform is the "salesman ban" for Lending Service Providers (LSPs) from November 1, 2025. LSPs are now barred from biased promotions for preferred Regulated Entities (REs). Multi-lender platforms must display all matching loan offers objectively, avoiding "dark patterns." REs assume full responsibility for fair market conduct. Lenders must provide complete upfront information, including a prominent Key Fact Statement (KFS) detailing APR and all charges for informed consent.

The Directions formalize RE-LSP relationships via mandatory contracts, requiring REs to perform enhanced due diligence and periodic reviews. Crucially, REs remain entirely responsible and liable for all LSP actions, affirming that financial duty of care cannot be delegated. All customer complaints related to Digital Lending Applications (DLAs) must be handled directly by the RE.

Strict data norms enforce minimization and explicit consent. DLAs cannot access sensitive mobile data (contacts, call logs); any temporary access, e.g., camera for KYC, needs explicit, audited consent. Borrowers can withdraw consent and request data deletion. All borrower data must be stored on Indian servers, with data processed abroad deleted and repatriated within 24 hours to enhance supervisory control.

These DL Directions represent a significant shift toward a governance-heavy model, increasing compliance burdens and operational costs for both REs and LSPs. REs must invest in robust internal systems, while LSPs face marketing restrictions and strict data practices. The overarching goal is to boost consumer confidence and transparency by ensuring LSPs act as neutral aggregators, firmly embedding digital innovation within India's consumer protection framework.

title: Land Acquisition Arbitration and Writ Jurisdiction: Constitutional Limitations in the Wake of Suryadev Pathak vs. Union of India
description:
The Allahabad High Court's judgment in Suryadev Pathak vs. Union of India elucidates the jurisdictional limitations of constitutional courts when statutory remedies are available. The case stemmed from Suryadev Pathak, a landowner, seeking enhanced compensation for land acquired under the National Highways Act, 1956, for the Bharat Mala Scheme. Dissatisfied with the initial compensation, Pathak invoked the arbitration mechanism specified in Section 3G(5) of the Act.

When the appointed arbitrator delayed rendering a decision for over two years, Pathak filed a writ petition under Article 226, alleging violations of his constitutional rights (Articles 14, 21, 300-A) and seeking expeditious resolution. The respondents countered, arguing that the High Court lacked jurisdiction as the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (A&C Act), provides a comprehensive framework, including provisions for timeline extensions exclusively by designated civil courts, not constitutional courts.

The High Court's analysis centered on the maintainability of writ jurisdiction when alternative statutory remedies exist, and the validity of mandating arbitration after statutory timelines expire. The court reasoned that upon the expiration of timelines prescribed by the A&C Act, specifically Section 29A, an arbitrator's mandate ceases. Consequently, any subsequent proceedings for timeline extensions must be adjudicated by competent civil courts, not through extraordinary writ jurisdiction, to prevent undermining legislative schemes and encouraging forum shopping.

The court dismissed the writ petition, establishing three fundamental principles: arbitration under Section 3G(5) of the NH Act is governed by the A&C Act; constitutional courts cannot exercise writ jurisdiction where specific and efficacious statutory remedies exist; and only competent civil courts possess the authority to extend arbitration timelines after an arbitrator's mandate expires. This judgment reinforces the integrity of specialized legislative frameworks, emphasizing the primacy of statutory arbitration over extraordinary constitutional intervention in land acquisition disputes.

title: Clock-Out Forever: How NCLT Told Ex-Workers That Missing the CIRP Deadline Means Missing the Money
description:
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) Mumbai recently dismissed claims by former employees of Indo Global Soft Solutions and Technologies Pvt. Ltd., delivering a critical judicial pronouncement on the strict adherence to statutory timelines within the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). Six former employees sought judicial intervention for unpaid salaries and dues, but their claims, submitted on October 25, 2023, were significantly past the initial deadline of May 4, 2022, and crucially, after the Committee of Creditors had already approved a resolution plan.

The applicants contended ignorance of the CIRP process and deadlines. However, the NCLT unequivocally ruled that the public announcement made pursuant to IBC regulations constituted "deemed knowledge." Further, their previous engagement with the Indian Institute of Insolvency Professionals contradicted their claims of unawareness. The Tribunal's decision was heavily influenced by Supreme Court precedents, which consistently emphasize the responsibility of stakeholders to remain vigilant and compliant with established IBC timelines.

Dismissing the applications, the NCLT reinforced the fundamental principle that timely claims submission is paramount. It emphasized that entertaining such belated applications would contravene the essential spirit and structure of the IBC, potentially undermining the integrity and efficiency of the entire resolution process and prolonging it unnecessarily. This ruling serves as a definitive precedent, highlighting that all stakeholders, including employees, must exercise due diligence, remain informed, and be proactive in protecting their interests within the designated time frames, as claims of ignorance do not constitute valid grounds for exemption from statutory timelines.

title: India’s Four Labour Codes: A Transformational Reform for the Nation’s Workforce
description:
On November 21, 2025, the Government of India implemented four consolidated Labour Codes (on Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions), replacing 29 fragmented colonial-era laws. This historic reform modernizes India's labour ecosystem, aligns it with global standards, and aims to ensure social justice and protection for all workers.

The previous labour framework was outdated, complex, and struggled to accommodate new employment forms like gig and platform work. It created significant compliance burdens for employers and left vast sections of the workforce, including informal, gig, platform, and contract workers, without uniform protections like minimum wages, social security, or formal appointment letters.

The new codes introduce several core reforms: mandatory appointment letters for all workers, universal social security coverage (PF, ESIC) extending to gig and platform workers with portable Aadhaar-linked Universal Account Numbers, and a statutory National Floor Wage ensuring minimum pay. They mandate timely wage payments, provide free annual health check-ups for workers over 40, and permit women to work night shifts and in all occupations with consent and safety measures. Compliance is significantly simplified with a single registration, pan-India license, and single return system, while dispute resolution mechanisms are streamlined.

These reforms offer substantial benefits across diverse categories: fixed-term employees now receive equal benefits and gratuity after one year; gig workers gain social security via aggregator contributions; and contract workers receive enhanced protections. The codes explicitly prohibit gender discrimination, ensure equal pay, and strengthen protections for youth, MSME workers, and those in hazardous industries. This comprehensive, pro-worker, pro-women, pro-youth, and pro-employment framework balances worker dignity and expanded social security with a more conducive environment for business growth and employment generation, supporting India's vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

title: CIRP Cannot Be Reopened Post CoC Approval, Rules NCLT
description:
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Mumbai Bench, has dismissed six belated claims from former employees of Indo Global Soft Solutions and Technologies Pvt. Ltd., reinforcing that the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) cannot be reopened post-Committee of Creditors (CoC) approval of a resolution plan.

The employees submitted their claims for unpaid salaries, PF, and other dues nearly eighteen months after the statutory deadline of May 4, 2022. Crucially, these claims were filed only after the CoC had twice approved a resolution plan and the Tribunal had already reserved orders on the second plan in August 2025.

The NCLT's decision rested on three pillars: strict adherence to IBC timelines (Regulation 12(1) and 13(1B)), finding a lack of bona fides in the applicants' conduct, and upholding the necessity of procedural discipline and finality in CIRP. The Tribunal rejected arguments of ignorance, noting employees had previously engaged professionally regarding claim rejections. It also emphasized that personal hardships, while regrettable, cannot override mandatory statutory obligations.

Citing Supreme Court precedents (RPS Infrastructure v. Mukul Kumar), the NCLT concluded that allowing such extremely delayed claims would derail the time-bound nature of the CIRP and erode commercial certainty. This ruling underscores that timeliness is a substantive cornerstone of the insolvency framework, preventing tactical disruptions and strengthening the integrity of the resolution process.

title: Preserving Truth In The Digital Era: Blockchain As The Next Guardian Of Evidence Integrity
description:
This article explores the transformative potential of blockchain technology in reforming India’s property registration system, as spotlighted by the Supreme Court’s Samiullah v. State of Bihar (2025) judgment. The Court invalidated Bihar’s restrictive requirement of mutation proof for property registration, reaffirming the legal distinction between registration and ownership. This pivotal ruling highlighted the urgent need for systemic reforms, positioning blockchain as a powerful solution for achieving transparent, tamper-proof, and conclusive land title records.

Blockchain offers a decentralized ledger that guarantees the immutability, transparency, and security of property records. Every entry is cryptographically linked, making data practically tamper-proof once recorded. Integrating blockchain with cadastral maps and revenue records can enhance transparency, drastically reduce fraudulent practices, and lower property-related disputes. The technology's ability to provide a verifiable, time-stamped audit trail also strengthens institutional trust, simplifies title searches, and ensures long-term preservation of evidence, addressing concerns about centralized system vulnerabilities.

Beyond land records, blockchain could safeguard court filings, government orders, and contracts, bridging the gap between technological capability and legal certainty. The Samiullah ruling signals a paradigm shift, inviting policymakers and technologists to develop a verifiable digital chain of custody. Embracing blockchain represents a pivotal moment in modernizing property law, securing the integrity of justice, and ensuring that truth in the digital age remains as unassailable as it is on paper.

title: Judicial Intervention And The Seat Of Arbitration: Balancing Autonomy And Justice In India
description:
The "seat of arbitration" traditionally defines the juridical home of proceedings and the supervising courts, typically limiting judicial interference. However, recent Indian cases illustrate an evolving landscape, demonstrating a nuanced approach where courts balance party autonomy with the need for justice-oriented flexibility.

In Engineering Projects (India) Ltd. v. MSA Global LLC, the Delhi High Court granted an interim injunction, halting a Singapore-seated arbitration due to concerns over procedural fairness and arbitrator bias. This rare intervention signals that party autonomy is not absolute, allowing Indian courts to act as guardians of justice in extraordinary circumstances.

Conversely, in Rhutikumari v. Zanmai Labs Pvt. Ltd., the Madras High Court granted interim relief concerning domestic cryptocurrency assets in a Singapore-seated arbitration. The court reasoned that intervention was justified because the cause of action and the property were located in India, highlighting a willingness to protect domestic interests.

Together, these cases reveal an emerging hybrid model in Indian arbitration jurisprudence. While the courts of the chosen seat generally retain supervisory control, Indian courts may exercise exceptional, limited intervention. This intervention is applied either to safeguard procedural fairness and prevent irreparable harm (as seen in Engineering Projects) or to protect domestic assets and interests (as in Rhutikumari). This approach ensures that the seat doctrine provides predictability and autonomy without sacrificing justice, reflecting India's pragmatic integration of global norms with equitable safeguards.

title: Unconditional Stay Only in Exceptional Cases: Supreme Court Clarifies Section 36(3)
description:
The Supreme Court of India, in Popular Caterers v. Ameet Mehta & Ors., clarified the principles governing the grant of stays on arbitral awards, particularly monetary ones, under Section 36(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court set aside a Bombay High Court order that had granted an unconditional stay on the execution of a ₹4-crore arbitral award, deeming it an exceptional relief granted without justifying circumstances.

The Bombay High Court had erroneously undertaken an extensive, premature merits review, finding the award's findings "perverse" at the interim stage. The Supreme Court emphasized that an unconditional stay is permissible only in truly exceptional situations, such as when an award is prima facie induced by fraud or corruption, or is patently illegal, non-existent, or wholly without jurisdiction. It noted that no such allegations were raised by the award debtors, and the High Court had failed to consider the protective purpose of Section 36(3) to secure the award holder.

Consequently, the Supreme Court directed the award debtors to deposit the principal amount of ₹4 crore with the Bombay High Court within eight weeks, for investment in a fixed-deposit account. The stay on the award was made conditional upon this deposit. The Court also instructed the Bombay High Court to expedite the disposal of the pending Section 34 petitions within six months. This ruling reinforces India's pro-enforcement arbitration framework, restricts premature merits reviews at the interim stage, and prevents award debtors from frustrating enforcement through unwarranted unconditional stays, thereby safeguarding the interests of award holders.

title: The Scent Of Innovation: Reinventing Tyres For A Refreshing Driving Experience
description:
India's Trade Marks Registry has made a historic move by accepting Sumitomo Rubber Industries' application for an olfactory trademark—a floral rose fragrance for tyres. This landmark decision expands Indian intellectual property law to include sensory branding, moving beyond conventional visual marks.

The journey to registration was marked by procedural controversy, with the Registry initially citing distinctiveness concerns, then abruptly shifting to claims of technological limitations in examining smell marks. Sumitomo, however, asserted that the Trade Marks Act mandates examination based on graphical representation and distinctiveness, not administrative system constraints.

The applicant successfully demonstrated both inherent distinctiveness, due to the arbitrary nature of a rose scent on tyres, and acquired distinctiveness from decades of continuous use since 1995. They argued the mark is easily recognizable by the "man of average intelligence and imperfect recollection." A significant hurdle, graphical representation, was overcome with a groundbreaking 7-dimensional vector model, developed with experts from IIIT Allahabad, meeting the clear, precise, and objective standards set by international precedents like Siekmann.

Shri Pravin Anand, acting as amicus curiae, provided impartial expertise, emphasizing the mark's distinctiveness and the acceptability of such non-functional scent marks in other jurisdictions. The Registry's final reasoning adopted a flexible interpretation of graphical representation, accepting the scientific model, and recognizing the arbitrary nature and inherent distinctiveness of the rose scent. This progressive stance, influenced by global practices, ensures non-traditional marks are not excluded solely due to representational challenges if statutory criteria are met.

This pioneering case, a testament to collaborative excellence spanning law and science, broadens intellectual property protections in India. It positions the nation among global leaders in recognizing smell as a powerful and unique brand identifier, paving the way for a new sensory dimension within trademark law.

title: India’s New Space Age: How A ₹1,000-Crore VC Fund And Indian Space Laws Are Powering The Next Frontier Of Start-Ups
description:
India's space sector is undergoing a profound transformation, shifting from state-led exploration to a market-driven ecosystem empowered by private startups. This new era is fundamentally driven by the operationalization of a ₹1,000-crore Space Venture Capital Fund and a robust, evolving legal framework, aiming to establish India as a global hub for space innovation.

The fund, a joint initiative by IN-SPACe and SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd., provides crucial risk capital, targeting approximately 40 high-potential startups over five years with investments ranging from ₹10-60 crore. This financial impetus complements a comprehensive regulatory environment. Key policy pillars include the Indian Space Policy 2023, which opens the entire space value chain to private participation and redefines roles for ISRO (R&D) and IN-SPACe as a single-window authority. The anticipated Space Activities Bill will further solidify this legal framework, addressing licensing, liability, and intellectual property. Recent reforms in 2024 also permit significant Foreign Direct Investment, up to 100% in certain sub-sectors, attracting global capital and collaboration.

These strategic initiatives are designed to propel India's space economy from its current US $8.4 billion to a projected US $44 billion by 2033. This growth is expected to foster innovation across launch systems, satellite manufacturing, data applications for various sectors, and in-space services. While challenges like the pending Space Activities Bill and clearer liability frameworks remain, this powerful synergy of capital and policy marks a pivotal moment, transforming India into a "space-startup superpower" driven by "Law-enabled Innovation."

title: Constitution Day 2025: Strengthening Democracy Through All Citizens, Especially Youth
description:
India commemorates Constitution Day on November 26, celebrating the adoption of its Constitution in 1949. This day underscores the nation's core principles: democracy, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity, and unity. It serves as a powerful reminder of the Constitution's paramount role in safeguarding democracy and fostering national unity and harmony.

The Constitution's monumental creation was led by visionary Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, who ensured the embodiment of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity, alongside protections against social discrimination like untouchability. Constitution Day honors these framers, presenting the document not just as a legal text but as a living guide upholding democratic governance and fundamental individual rights.

The observance inspires citizens, especially youth, to engage actively with constitutional values through activities such as reading the Preamble, debates, and seminars. It highlights fundamental rights and duties, cultivating a strong commitment to the rule of law and social justice. Youth play a critical role in promoting cultural respect, community dialogues, and spreading awareness, thereby strengthening democracy and national unity.

Facing challenges like social inequalities and communal tensions, Constitution Day acts as a vital call to action for all citizens. It particularly urges the youth to embrace their constitutional rights and duties, becoming guardians of democratic ideals. Their active participation is crucial to champion inclusivity, combat discrimination, and foster societal unity, ensuring the Constitution's vision endures and thrives for generations to come.

title: Streamlining Insolvency Appointments: IBBI’s Second (2025) Guidelines for Professionals
description:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) released its Second Guidelines (2025) to streamline the appointment of Insolvency Professionals (IPs) as Interim Resolution Professionals, Liquidators, Resolution Professionals, and Bankruptcy Trustees. Effective for a six-month cycle from January 1 to June 30, 2026, these guidelines aim to eliminate administrative delays by pre-assembling zonewise and benchwise panels, operationalizing specific sections of the IBC 2016.

Eligibility for the panel requires no pending disciplinary proceedings or recent convictions, an unconditional expression of interest (Form A submitted by December 22, 2025), and an Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) valid until June 30, 2026. IPs must consent to serve any assigned role or debtor and declare their sector experience. The common panel for all four roles, compiled by December 31, 2025, is disaggregated zonewise/benchwise, sorted by ongoing assignments and registration chronology. Insolvency Professional Entities are exempt from zone restrictions, eligible for pan-India appointments.

Crucially, consent to be on the panel is irrevocable, signifying an undertaking to accept appointments. Unjustified refusal leads to immediate panel removal and a six-month debarment. Professionals must also maintain their registration and AFA during the panel's validity. While the Adjudicating Authority retains flexibility to appoint outside the panel if warranted, these guidelines enhance transparency and accountability. They replace the May 2025 framework, ensuring faster and more predictable insolvency appointments from January 2026, with clear obligations for professionals.

title: Seven Day Cure Command: Supreme Court Halts NCLT Rejection for Skipping Section 7(5)(b) Notice
description:
The Supreme Court, in Civil Appeal No. 11766 of 2025, has definitively ruled that before rejecting a financial creditor's Section 7 petition under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the adjudicating authority must first issue a specific seven-day healing notice to the applicant under the second proviso to Section 7(5)(b). Failure to provide this direct notice constitutes a jurisdictional error. This landmark judgment stemmed from a dispute involving HDFC Bank Limited and the corporate debtor, Live-in Aqua Solutions Private Limited.

The case highlighted a procedural lapse where HDFC Bank's petition contained defects, including an affidavit predating the verification date. The NCLT Registry refused registration after publishing a consolidated defect sheet, but no separate, specific seven-day notice under the Code's proviso was served directly to the bank. While the NCLAT later acknowledged the procedural error, the Supreme Court emphasized the mandatory nature of this notice, stating that a mere consolidated listing of defects is insufficient.

The Supreme Court clarified that a defective affidavit is a curable irregularity, not a fatal flaw that renders the application non est. It reiterated that procedure should aid justice, not obstruct it. Although the NCLAT correctly identified the procedural lapse, the Supreme Court chided it for not directing the bank to file a fresh, compliant affidavit. Consequently, the Court mandated HDFC Bank to cure all defects, including filing a new affidavit, within seven days from the judgment date. Following this, the NCLT will proceed to decide the petition on its merits.

This ruling underscores the imperative for tribunals to uphold procedural safeguards, branding the absence of the specific seven-day notice a jurisdictional flaw. It ensures that financial creditors are afforded a clear opportunity to rectify defects, reinforcing the principle of "cure first, reject later" within the IBC framework.

title: IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Personal Guarantors to Corporate Debtors) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025 Makes Accuracy and Punctuality Non-Negotiable for Resolution Professionals
description:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) introduced the (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, on November 20, 2025, to address chronic issues of late and inaccurate filings by Resolution Professionals (RPs) in the insolvency resolution process for personal guarantors. This crucial amendment, effective immediately, inserts a new Regulation 23 into the 2019 Regulations, fundamentally transforming best practices into statutory duties and aiming to enhance creditor confidence and accelerate judicial proceedings.

Regulation 23 mandates strict procedural discipline. RPs are now legally obliged to file all prescribed Forms and their enclosures electronically on the IBBI's designated platform by specified deadlines, allowing no discretion. Furthermore, RPs must certify that all submitted information is true, complete, and not misleading, effectively ending any "file-now-correct-later" approach. Non-compliance triggers an automatic penalty of ₹500 per Form for each calendar month of delay, applicable to initial filings, corrections, or updates. Beyond monetary fines, the IBBI is empowered to refuse to issue or renew an RP's "Authorisation for Assignment" for failures related to filing, accuracy, or timeliness, posing a significant professional and existential threat. These reforms leverage a central digital platform and stringent penalties to ensure data integrity, compress timelines, and deliver faster outcomes for all stakeholders.

title: Menstrual Leave Becomes a Legal Entitlement in Karnataka Workplaces: No Certificate, No Carry-Over
description:
On November 20, 2025, Karnataka's Labour Department issued Government Order No. LD 466 LET 2023, establishing menstrual leave as a binding statutory entitlement. This mandate grants women workers aged 18-52 one paid leave day per menstrual cycle, capped at twelve days annually. Significantly, it is self-certification based, eliminating the need for medical proof.

The entitlement stemmed from extensive deliberations by a multi-stakeholder committee formed in January 2024, followed by public consultation that showed strong support. The order invokes five central and state labour statutes, ensuring pan-sectoral coverage for all registered establishments and women employees, including contractual and outsourced workers.

Key features of the leave include its compensatory and wage-protected nature, with monetary liability resting solely on the employer. It cannot be offset against other leave types. A statutory cap of twelve days per calendar year applies, with unused leave lapsing monthly—it cannot be accumulated, encashed, or carried forward. Employees simply need to intimate their intention to avail the leave within the same month. The order took immediate effect on November 20, 2025, requiring establishments to update systems and face penalties for non-compliance. This marks a pivotal shift from discretionary welfare to a statutory right, emphasizing employee dignity and administrative simplicity.

title: SWIFT 2.0 Goes Live: FSSAI–CBIC Integration Reshapes Legal Architecture of Food-Import Clearance
description:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) have jointly announced the pilot launch of SWIFT 2.0, an upgraded interface designed to integrate food-safety oversight with customs control. This new system embeds FSSAI’s Food Import Clearance System (FICS) directly into CBIC’s ICEGATE portal, replacing SWIFT 1.0 with a real-time, two-way data conduit. The initiative aims to compress regulatory clearance times, eliminate duplicative filings, and reinforce the Government's commitments to "Ease of Doing Business" and "Digital India."

The primary objective is to streamline food import processes by providing a single-window design where importers can obtain the FSSAI No-Objection Certificate directly through the SWIFT portal. This eliminates the need for parallel applications, thereby reducing human interface, shortening cargo dwell time, and lowering the cost of doing business, all while maintaining transparency and accountability within the system.

The pilot phase is strategically confined to four high-volume inland container depots—Dadri, Star Track, Albatross, and Patparganj—selected based on cargo density, existing digital infrastructure, and the presence of accredited laboratories. This approach ensures early identification of systemic bottlenecks without disrupting the wider import ecosystem. Upon successful validation, SWIFT 2.0 will be rolled out nationally to all major food-import entry points, underscoring India’s commitment to efficient, transparent, and technology-driven food-import processes and a strengthened food-safety ecosystem.

title: IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025: An analysis
description:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) promulgated the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Professionals) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025, effective November 21, 2025. Issued under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, these regulations introduce critical amendments to the existing framework governing Insolvency Professionals (IPs), aiming to enhance efficiency and accountability within the insolvency resolution process.

A significant change is the insertion of Regulation 7B, establishing a quantitative ceiling on assignments. Individual IPs (not insolvency professional entities) are now restricted to a maximum of ten concurrent assignments, covering roles such as Interim Resolution Professional, Resolution Professional, and Liquidator. Within this limit, no more than three assignments can pertain to processes with admitted claims exceeding INR 1000 crore each. IPs exceeding these thresholds upon commencement are prohibited from accepting new assignments until their active portfolio falls below the prescribed limits.

Furthermore, amendments to the Code of Conduct (First Schedule) include replacing "the approval of the Board" with "the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority" in Clause 6, thereby transferring sanctioning power from the IBBI to the National Company Law Tribunal. Clause 22 has also been omitted. These amendments signify a shift from self-declared workload management to a hard statutory ceiling, designed to mitigate timeline slippages and enhance fiduciary oversight. Stakeholders are advised to audit existing mandates and integrate these revised thresholds into their operational frameworks to ensure regulatory compliance.

title: IBBI Discussion Paper, 14 November 2025: Proposed Re-calibration of Valuation Architecture under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
description:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) has released a discussion paper addressing systemic issues in the valuation process, including non-uniform reports, divergent standards, an asset-centric definition of fair value, disproportionate costs for small debtors, and the absence of an integrated enterprise-level figure. These issues lead to litigation and reduced stakeholder confidence. The paper proposes five key amendments to subordinate legislation to enhance transparency, consistency, and predictability in fair and liquidation value determinations.

Firstly, to improve consistency and auditability, the Board recommends an omnibus enabling clause to prescribe standardized report templates and obligatory documentation protocols via circulars for all insolvency proceedings. These templates will be modular, allowing for asset-class specific schedules while maintaining a common master format.

Secondly, the paper proposes unifying valuation standards. It suggests replacing current references to "internationally accepted valuation standards" or the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017, with "valuation standards as specified by the Board," thus granting the IBBI authority to promulgate a single, consistent standard.

Thirdly, the definition of "fair value" is set to undergo a significant conceptual change. The revised definition will require valuers to estimate the corporate debtor's realizable value as an economic unit, incorporating tangible and intangible assets (e.g., brand, goodwill) and the synergistic premium of a going-concern transaction, rather than merely discrete assets.

Fourthly, to mitigate the burden on small estates, the paper suggests a calibrated derogation allowing for the appointment of a single registered valuer per asset class for corporate debtors with an annual turnover not exceeding ₹500 crore or those qualifying as MSMEs. The Committee of Creditors retains discretion to mandate a second set with stated reasons.

Finally, to synthesize individual asset-class estimates into a comprehensive enterprise-level figure, the paper introduces a "Coordinator Valuer." This individual will integrate underlying valuations to furnish an Aggregate Fair Value (AFV) for the corporate debtor, with a mechanism for averaging AFVs and addressing significant deviations. An equivalent system is proposed for liquidation value.

Stakeholder comments are invited on these proposals by December 7, 2025. If implemented, these amendments are expected to establish a rule-based, verifiable, enterprise-centric valuation architecture, thereby minimizing informational friction, curtailing litigation risk, and advancing the Code's objective of value maximization.

title: Enforcing A 92-Year-Old Decree: The Supreme Court On Faith, Proof, And Possession
description:
In 2025, the Supreme Court of India resolved a 92-year-old temple dispute concerning Sangalappa Swamy, stemming from a 1933 compromise decree. The case involved the Kapadam and Kamatam families, both from the Kuruba community, who disputed hereditary rights to worship the deity and possess sacred items. The original decree mandated alternating idol possession, rotating ritual duties, a ₹2,000 payment from the Kamatams, and the appointment of trustees.

Decades later, the Kapadam families initiated an execution petition, accusing the Kamatams of breaching the rotation agreement and unlawfully retaining the idols. The Kamatams argued that the 1933 decree's key conditions, including the payment and trustee appointments, were never implemented, and thus, the arrangement itself was never put into practice.
