This decision underscores the social justice intent of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, positioning motor insurance as a public welfare instrument rather than merely a private contract. The core of the judgment relies on the "pay and recover" doctrine, ensuring immediate compensation for victims while preserving the insurer's right to seek recovery from the vehicle owner for proven contractual violations.

The case originated from a fatal motor accident involving a bus, owned by K. Nagendra and insured by New India Assurance Co. Ltd., which was allegedly plying outside its permitted route. While the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal awarded compensation, the insurer challenged it, citing a fundamental breach of policy conditions. The central legal question before the Apex Court was whether a route permit violation absolves the insurer from third-party liability or if it must still compensate victims before seeking recovery from the vehicle owner.

The Supreme Court emphatically stated that an insurer cannot escape liability to third parties solely because the vehicle operated outside its sanctioned route. It emphasized that the essence of compulsory insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act is to prevent victims from being left uncompensated due to technical defaults. The Court reiterated the "pay and recover" mechanism, directing the insurer to first disburse compensation to the victims and then recover the amount from the vehicle owner if the policy breach is established. This approach judiciously balances the protection of third-party rights with the insurer's contractual interests. While prioritizing victim compensation, the Court also clarified that the insurer's obligations are not unlimited, respecting contractual boundaries where liability clearly falls outside the agreed framework.

Consequently, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, directing New India Assurance Co. Ltd. to pay the awarded compensation to the victims' dependents and subsequently recover the sum from the vehicle owner, K. Nagendra. This judgment reinforces the imperative of prompt compensation for accident victims, regardless of technical infractions, while also ensuring contractual accountability for vehicle owners who violate permit conditions. The ruling solidifies the integrity of India's motor accident compensation system by embodying both judicial empathy for victims and fairness for insurers.

title: Supreme Court Reaffirms Protection to Bona Fide Purchasers in VAT Transactions: Commissioner, Trade & Tax.
description:
The Supreme Court of India, in The Commissioner, Trade and Tax, Delhi v. M/s Shanti Kiran India (P) Ltd., has decisively reaffirmed protection for bona fide purchasing dealers under the Delhi Value Added Tax Act, 2004 (DVAT Act). The Court dismissed the Department's appeals, upholding the Delhi High Court's stance that Input Tax Credit (ITC) cannot be denied to genuine purchasers solely because the selling dealer, despite being registered at the time of transaction, subsequently defaulted on depositing the collected tax with the government. This ruling carries binding legal significance, reinforcing established interpretations and safeguarding genuine business transactions.

The dispute originated from the Department's denial of ITC to purchasing dealers, including M/s Shanti Kiran India (P) Ltd., who had bought goods from validly registered sellers, paid VAT, and possessed proper tax invoices. The Department argued that since the selling dealers later had their registrations cancelled and failed to remit the collected VAT to the treasury, the corresponding ITC claimed by the purchasers was inadmissible.

The Delhi High Court had previously "read down" Section 9(2)(g) of the DVAT Act, which stated that ITC would not be allowed if the tax payable by the selling dealer had not been deposited. The High Court reasoned that this provision should not penalize bona fide purchasing dealers acting in good faith without collusion or fraud. It emphasized that the Department's remedy lies against the defaulting seller, not the innocent buyer, to avoid rendering the provision arbitrary and unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court concurred, finding no reason to interfere with the Delhi High Court's judgment. It observed that denying ITC in such circumstances would be unjustified, especially given its earlier confirmation of similar High Court reasoning. The Court concluded that the appeals lacked merit, thereby upholding the right of bona fide dealers to claim ITC.

This concise yet impactful order holds substantial jurisprudential value. It clarifies the scope of Section 9(2)(g), ensuring that honest taxpayers are protected from the defaults of their sellers, provided they have conducted genuine transactions with registered dealers and possess valid documentation. The ruling aligns with broader principles of "buyer protection" seen in other indirect tax regimes, such as GST, strengthening the continuity of judicial thought favouring equity, proportionality, and constitutional fairness in tax administration. For businesses, it provides crucial clarity and reassurance that compliance obligations will not extend beyond what is reasonable and just.

title: Supreme Court Clarifies: Redeemable Preference Shareholders Are Not Financial Creditors Under IBC
description:
The Supreme Court of India, in the case of EPC Constructions India Limited (Through Its Liquidator) v. Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Limited, has definitively ruled that holders of Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares (CRPS) are not to be treated as financial creditors under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). This landmark decision reinforces the statutory distinction between share capital and debt, asserting that preference shareholders are investors, not lenders, and their claims for redemption cannot constitute a "financial debt" to trigger insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC.

The dispute originated from EPC Constructions India Limited (EPCC) converting outstanding receivables of ₹250 crore from Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Limited into 8% CRPS. When Matix failed to redeem these shares due to a lack of profits or fresh issue proceeds, EPCC's liquidator filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC, contending that Matix had defaulted on a "financial debt." Both the NCLT and NCLAT dismissed this petition, leading to the appeal before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court's analysis highlighted several key points. It affirmed that preference shares constitute part of a company's share capital under the Companies Act, 2013, and do not represent loans. Therefore, even if redemption is due, failure to redeem does not transform shareholders into creditors. The Court emphasized that redemption under Section 55 of the Companies Act is contingent upon the availability of distributable profits or proceeds from a fresh issue of shares, which Matix lacked. Furthermore, the conversion of receivables into shares extinguished the original debt, making it a conscious equity investment rather than a disguised loan. The Court also rejected arguments based on accounting treatment classifying CRPS as "unsecured loans," stating that accounting standards cannot override the legal nature of a transaction. Finally, it clarified that the "commercial effect of borrowing" test under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC applies only to genuine debt transactions involving the disbursal and time value of money, which equity instruments like CRPS inherently lack.

This ruling by the Supreme Court critically reinforces the distinction between equity and debt within corporate finance. It safeguards the IBC from being invoked as a mechanism for recovering equity investments and underscores that share capital retains its equity character until lawfully redeemed in accordance with the Companies Act. The judgment contributes to strengthening corporate governance by promoting investor discipline and preserving the integrity of corporate capital structures.

title: Delhi High Court Upholds Crocs’ Design and Brand Integrity in Questsole Dispute
description:
The Delhi High Court has issued an ex-parte ad-interim injunction in favor of Crocs Inc. and its subsidiary, affirming the protection of their extensive intellectual property rights against Sagar Doijode, trading as Questsole, and others. The suit, filed before the Delhi High Court, sought a permanent injunction for alleged infringement of Crocs' patents, trademarks, registered designs, and distinctive trade dress.

Crocs alleged that Questsole was manufacturing, advertising, and selling footwear and shoe charms that were identical or deceptively similar to their products. Specifically, the defendants were accused of infringing Patent No. IN 271337, which covers the system for attaching decorative accessories (Jibbitz) to shoes, and of copying the registered design No. 349374-001 for Crocs' iconic clog-style footwear. Furthermore, Questsole was found to be using deceptive marks like “CROCKS,” “CROC,” and “JIBIT,” infringing Crocs' registered trademarks “CROCS” and “JIBBITZ.” The defendants also imitated Crocs’ distinctive trade dress, characterized by the clogs' unique bulbous shape, ventilation holes, and back strap design, and posted disparaging videos online.

Justice Tejas Karia, after reviewing the evidence, determined that Crocs Inc. possessed substantial global goodwill, reputation, and valid intellectual property registrations. The Court observed that the defendants' actions, including the use of deceptively similar marks and designs, appeared to be a dishonest attempt to exploit Crocs’ established brand identity and create consumer confusion. A test purchase confirmed direct patent infringement, and the visual and structural resemblance between the defendants' products and Crocs' registered design and trade dress was deemed fraudulent imitation, leading to dilution of Crocs’ distinctiveness.

Based on these findings, the Delhi High Court concluded that Crocs Inc. had established a prima facie case for interim relief, with the balance of convenience lying in its favor and a risk of irreparable harm if an injunction was not granted. Consequently, the Court restrained the defendants from using the infringing marks, manufacturing or selling products embodying Crocs' patented system, imitating its registered design, or copying the distinctive trade dress of Crocs’ geometric clogs. The matter is scheduled for further hearing on February 16, 2026.

title: Delhi High Court Affirms Validity of Full and Final Settlement in Subcontract Recovery Dispute
description:
The Delhi High Court recently issued a significant judgment affirming the validity of a full and final settlement in a subcontract recovery dispute between M/S BS Enviro N Infracon Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant) and VIJ Contracts Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent). The core of the case involved the Appellant's claim for an outstanding amount of Rs. 50,41,835/- related to an 800 KLD Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) subcontract, following the Trial Court's dismissal of its recovery suit. The central question revolved around whether a document signed by the parties constituted a conclusive settlement of all claims.

The dispute originated from the Appellant subcontracting its services to the Respondent for an STP project with a total contract value of Rs. 1,28,80,000/-. After receiving partial payments, the Appellant initiated MSME Samadhaan proceedings for a claimed balance of Rs. 50,41,835/-. A pivotal meeting on September 26, 2019, resulted in a document recording a net balance of Rs. 14,68,165/-, subject to the Appellant withdrawing its MSME notice. The Respondent issued cheques for this agreed amount, which the Appellant encashed. However, the Appellant failed to withdraw the MSME notice and continued to pursue further claims, which were subsequently dismissed by an arbitral award and later by the Trial Court.

The Appellant contended that the September 26, 2019 document merely recorded "on account" payments to maintain the contract, not a full discharge of liabilities. They also sought release of unbilled contract value and retention amounts, asserting substantial performance. Conversely, the Respondent argued that the document represented a full and final settlement and a novation of prior obligations under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, with the encashment signifying acceptance.

The High Court meticulously examined the evidence, concluding that the September 26, 2019 document, acknowledged by the Appellant's Director, clearly established a full and final settlement. The Court held that the Appellant's act of encashing the cheques, coupled with the contemporaneous records, constituted "accord and satisfaction" and a "novation" of all accrued claims under Sections 62 and 63 of the Indian Contract Act. It emphasized that voluntary acceptance of a lesser sum in satisfaction of a claim bars subsequent pursuit of the balance. The Court dismissed the Appellant's "on account" argument as inconsistent with the signed agreement and their subsequent actions. Furthermore, claims for unbilled contract value and retention amounts were rejected, as the Appellant failed to demonstrate substantial performance—having supplied materials but not completed essential installation, testing, or commissioning—or that the conditions for release of retention had matured.

In conclusion, the Delhi High Court upheld the Trial Court's decision, affirming that the settlement reached on September 26, 2019, effectively discharged all prior claims and barred the Appellant from pursuing further recovery for those matters.

title: No Shield of Rule 9(5) When Bank Suppresses Court Order: Telangana HC Refunds ₹2.16 Crore to Auction Purchaser
description:
The Telangana High Court has quashed the forfeiture of a ₹2.16 crore deposit made by an auction purchaser, directing the Union Bank of India to refund the amount. This ruling, under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act), underscores the critical importance of transparency and fairness in bank auctions. The court found that the bank had suppressed a material court order restraining the sale confirmation, exhibiting a lack of probity and engaging in unjust enrichment.

The petitioner, an auction purchaser, emerged as the highest bidder with a ₹8.65 crore bid and deposited 25% of the sale consideration (₹2.16 crore) on March 15, 2023. Unbeknownst to the petitioner, a High Court order issued on March 20, 2023, specifically restrained the bank from confirming the sale. Despite this judicial restraint, the bank neither informed the petitioner of the order nor halted its demand for the remaining payment. Subsequently, the bank forfeited the deposit on June 13, 2023, citing the petitioner's failure to pay the balance within the stipulated time.

The High Court meticulously examined the facts, concluding that while the petitioner was aware of general DRT proceedings, the specific High Court restraint order was deliberately withheld. The court held that Rule 9(5) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, which governs forfeiture, presupposes a transparent process and cannot be invoked as a shield when the bank itself suppresses crucial information. It further determined that the bank's conduct amounted to unjust enrichment and that the deliberate non-disclosure constituted exceptional circumstances, justifying the maintainability of the writ petition despite the existence of alternative remedies.

Drawing support from precedents emphasizing the bank's duty of due diligence and disclosure, the court allowed the writ petition in part. It directed the Union Bank of India to refund the ₹2.16 crore within four weeks. However, it declined to issue a direction for accepting the balance payment or executing a sale certificate, acknowledging the complexities of the ongoing litigation surrounding the property. This judgment serves as a vital reminder to financial institutions that their powers under the SARFAESI Act must be exercised with utmost transparency and fairness, reinforcing the judiciary's role in safeguarding equitable conduct in commercial transactions.

title: Lull vs. Cessation: Supreme Court Defines “Carrying on Business” for Non-Residents
description:
In a landmark judgment concerning Pride Foramer S.A. v. Commissioner of Income Tax & Anr., the Supreme Court of India has provided essential clarification on the concept of "carrying on business" for non-resident companies. The core issue revolved around whether a non-resident entity, during a period without active contracts or a physical presence in India, could still be considered to be carrying on its business and thus be eligible to claim deductions for business expenditure under Section 37 and carry forward unabsorbed depreciation under Section 32(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. This ruling significantly impacts how business continuity is assessed, particularly for project-based industries in a globalized economy.

The appellant, Pride Foramer S.A., a French oil drilling company, had an "interregnum" period (1996-2000) after an initial 10-year contract expired in 1993, during which it had no active drilling operations in India. Despite this inactivity, the company maintained business correspondences with ONGC from its offices abroad and submitted a bid for a new oil exploration contract, which it eventually secured in 1998. While the Assessing Officer and CIT (Appeals) disallowed tax benefits, asserting the company was not "carrying on any business," the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) reversed these findings. The ITAT distinguished between a "temporary lull" and "cessation of business," recognizing the appellant's ongoing efforts. However, the High Court of Uttarakhand overturned the ITAT, linking "carrying on business" to the presence of a permanent office or an active contract in India.

The Supreme Court, overturning the High Court's decision, unequivocally affirmed that the appellant was indeed "carrying on business" during the relevant period. The Court emphasized that the company's continuous business correspondences and active bidding for new contracts demonstrated a clear "intention to carry on business" from the perspective of a prudent businessman, constituting a "lull in business" rather than a complete cessation. Crucially, the Supreme Court declared the High Court's linkage of "carrying on business" with the existence of a "permanent establishment" (PE) as "wholly fallacious." It clarified that while a PE is relevant for Double Tax Avoidance Agreements (DTAA), it is not a mandatory prerequisite under Indian tax law for a non-resident to be deemed as carrying on business and thus liable for tax on income from a "business connection in India." The Court further noted that the High Court's restrictive view was "wholly anachronistic" in the contemporary era of globalization and contrary to the principle of "ease of doing business."

This judgment provides much-needed clarity, adopting a pragmatic and commercially aware approach to tax law. By distinctly separating a temporary business lull from permanent cessation and delinking the concept of "carrying on business" from the rigid requirement of a physical "Permanent Establishment," the Supreme Court has set a vital precedent. The decision champions the intention and continuous efforts of an assessee, such as maintaining client relationships and bidding for new work, as integral to business continuity. This aligns Indian tax jurisprudence with global commercial realities, offering significant protection to businesses during unavoidable inactive periods and fostering an environment conducive to international trade and investment.

title: Supreme Court: Non-Resident Companies Liable to Tax in India Even Without Permanent Office
description:
The Supreme Court of India recently delivered a significant judgment in the case of Pride Foramer S.A. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, clarifying that non-resident companies can be deemed to be carrying on business in India even during periods of operational inactivity, thus remaining eligible for tax deductions and liable for tax on income accruing in India.

The case involved Pride Foramer S.A., a French offshore oil drilling company, which experienced a lull in active contracts between 1993 and 1999. During this interim, despite operating from foreign offices and having no active projects, the company engaged in business correspondence, submitted bids, incurred various business-related expenses, and claimed deductions for these along with unabsorbed depreciation. The Income Tax Department, however, disallowed these claims, asserting that the company had ceased business operations during this inactive period.

Reversing the High Court's decision, the Supreme Court affirmed the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal's view, distinguishing a "lull" from a "cessation" of business. The Court emphasized that a company's continuous intent and efforts to secure future contracts, such as submitting bids and maintaining business correspondence, demonstrate ongoing operations, irrespective of immediate contract acquisition. Crucially, the Court clarified that the absence of a permanent establishment or conducting business solely through foreign offices does not absolve a non-resident company from tax liability in India if income accrues or arises within the country. Consequently, the Court allowed the deduction of business expenses under Section 37 and permitted the carry-forward of unabsorbed depreciation under Section 32(2) of the Income Tax Act.

This landmark judgment adopts a pragmatic and modern approach to assessing non-resident companies, reinforcing the principle of "substance over form." It establishes that business continuity and entitlement to tax benefits are determined by a company's overarching conduct and intent, rather than merely by active contract periods or physical presence within India, thereby aligning with globalized trade dynamics.

title: Speak Now or Forever Hold Your Peace: Bombay HC Clears ICC, Denies Tarapur Doctor a Second Bite After Year-Long Silence Makes Waiver Win the POSH Fight
description:
The Bombay High Court has affirmed that silence during a sexual harassment inquiry can amount to a waiver of procedural objections, denying a doctor's petition to quash an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) report. In the case of Dr Shyam Bihari v. Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd., the court emphasized that participating in proceedings without protest precludes subsequent challenges to the ICC's composition or procedure, and reiterated the correct interpretation of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act).

Dr. Shyam Bihari, a Medical Officer at NPCIL's Tarapur site, faced an inquiry after a complaint of inappropriate behavior in July 2024. An ICC was swiftly constituted, headed by a woman medical officer of the same grade as Dr. Bihari, along with other members including an external expert. After recording statements and conducting an inquiry, the ICC, applying the "preponderance of probabilities" standard, concluded in December 2024 that the allegations were proven, despite an earlier preliminary note observing "insufficient evidence."

Instead of submitting a representation to the disciplinary authority, Dr. Bihari petitioned the High Court in August 2025, seeking to quash the proceedings. His primary arguments centered on the Presiding Officer not being senior in rank to him, the "external" member having a consultancy contract with NPCIL, and an apprehension of bias due to another member living in the same building as the complainant's father. He also referenced a Department of Personnel & Training memorandum regarding the seniority of inquiry officers in general disciplinary cases.

The High Court dismissed Dr. Bihari's petition, highlighting his year-long participation in the inquiry without raising any objections. Justice Bhobe, writing for the Bench, applied the cardinal rule of statutory interpretation, noting that Section 4(2)(a) of the POSH Act requires the Presiding Officer to be a "senior-level woman," not necessarily senior in rank to the accused. The court found no material evidence of the ENT surgeon being an employee or that the neighbor-member influenced the panel. Furthermore, it clarified that the October note was an interim assessment, and the December report applied the correct standard of proof. The court also reminded the petitioner that the POSH Act provides a self-contained appeal mechanism to a court or tribunal once the disciplinary authority issues final orders, making his writ petition premature.

This judgment serves as a critical reminder that procedural objections in an inquiry must be raised at the earliest opportunity. It reinforces that meticulously conducted ICC inquiries, adhering to the statutory checklist and principles of natural justice, will withstand judicial scrutiny, even if the Presiding Officer is not hierarchically senior to the accused, provided they meet the "senior-level woman" requirement. The ruling clears the path for NPCIL's disciplinary authority to proceed with determining the appropriate penalty.

title: When IBC Meets Electricity Act: Why Discoms Can’t Hold a New Owner to Ransom for Past Arrears
description:
The Allahabad High Court has decisively ruled on the pre-eminence of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) over the Electricity Act, 2003, in a case involving past electricity arrears. The court affirmed that power distribution companies (discoms) cannot compel new owners, who acquire assets through IBC liquidation auctions, to settle outstanding electricity bills of the former corporate debtor before providing a new connection. This judgment, M/s Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. Managing Director, PVVNL, reinforces the protection afforded to successful resolution applicants and auction purchasers from inheriting historical liabilities.

The dispute arose when Dharti Agro Industries purchased the assets of a liquidated company, M/s Chaudhary Ingots Pvt. Ltd., via an "as-is-where-is-whatever-there-is" auction under the IBC. Following the acquisition, the Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. (PVVNL) refused to grant a new electricity connection unless Dharti Agro paid ₹4.92 crore in arrears owed by the previous owner. This prompted Dharti Agro to seek legal recourse against the discom's demand.

Dharti Agro contended that Section 238 of the IBC, being a non-obstante clause, overrides any inconsistent provisions in the Electricity Act. They argued, supported by Supreme Court precedents, that a discom must participate in the IBC's liquidation process and adhere to its waterfall mechanism for debt recovery, rather than penalizing a new, unrelated owner. PVVNL, conversely, maintained that the Electricity Act, with its own non-obstante clauses, is a comprehensive code for electricity dues, and a statutory first charge on the premises meant that arrears were tied to the asset, citing the K.C. Ninan Supreme Court judgment.

The High Court concluded that the IBC, as a later special statute with a broad non-obstante clause (Section 238), prevails over the Electricity Act, applying the "last-in-time" doctrine. The court distinguished K.C. Ninan, noting it did not arise from an IBC liquidation. It held that PVVNL's appropriate path for recovering its dues was through the IBC's Section 53 waterfall mechanism, having already filed its claim with the liquidator, rather than using the electricity connection as leverage against the auction purchaser. Consequently, the court quashed PVVNL's coercive order and directed the immediate installation of the new electricity connection, clarifying that the discom's dues would be processed by the liquidator under the IBC framework.

This ruling reiterates the IBC's foundational role as a comprehensive framework designed to re-order creditor rights and insulate fresh investments from the baggage of the past. By preventing discoms from hindering the operationalization of assets due to previous owners' debts, the judgment significantly enhances the credibility of the insolvency process and instills confidence in auction purchasers that their acquired assets can be utilized without inherited financial encumbrances.

title: DoT Tightens Noose on Unused Transmitters, Issues Post Licence Disposal Playbook
description:
India's Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has issued a comprehensive guideline to resolve the ambiguity surrounding the disposal of wireless transmitting and receiving equipment upon the expiry of a Wireless Operating Licence (WOL). Effective immediately and applicable to all entities—private and public—possessing radiating hardware under WPC licenses, these stern guidelines establish clear accountability and strict timelines for equipment disposal, backed by the threat of prosecution under the Indian Telegraphy Act.

The guidelines prescribe varying disposal periods depending on the manner of licence expiry. For licensee-initiated cancellations, a 90-day window is provided to scrap, return, transfer the apparatus, or secure a Non-Destructive Possession Licence (NDPL), with a "deemed NDPL" cover during this period. In cases of simple non-renewal, a 30-day period is allotted for disposal, requiring a disposal certificate upload within seven days of completion, also with a deemed NDPL. The most abrupt scenario, government-induced termination due to breach of conditions, allows only 15 days for hardware removal and surrender, reflecting a heightened focus on spectrum security. Retaining equipment for future experiments necessitates obtaining a regular NDPL before the existing licence lapses, as no deemed grace period is extended for long-term storage.

Proof of disposal can be established by returning equipment to the original vendor or an authorised dealer, transferring it to another licensed entity with identical frequency clearance, or physically destroying it in the presence of a Wireless Monitoring Organisation (WMO) inspector or licensed dealer. Government laboratories may self-certify demolition but must inform WPC. Crucially, all disposed equipment, including circuit boards, batteries, and metal carcasses, must comply with the Environment Ministry's 2022 rules for telecom-specific e-waste, ensuring they reach only authorised recyclers.

Non-compliance with these new directives will be treated as a wilful violation, leading to "appropriate action" by the DoT, which could include fines, black-listing, and criminal prosecution under wireless statutes. The new playbook definitively shifts the full lifecycle liability for every radio chip onto the licence-holder, emphasizing that experimental frequencies are temporary leases on public property, and equipment must be promptly removed once the licence tenure concludes.

title: When Fees Stop the Fight: Bombay High Court Upholds Tribunal’s Power to Terminate Arbitration for Non Payment
description:
The Bombay High Court, in a ruling by Justice Manish Pitale, upheld an arbitral tribunal's decision to terminate arbitration claims under Section 38(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, due to a claimant's persistent non-payment of arbitrator fees. The case involved Marvel Sigma Homes Private Limited, whose claims were terminated while the respondents' counterclaim was allowed to proceed. Marvel Sigma challenged this decision via a writ petition, prompting a debate on the maintainability of such petitions, the tribunal's jurisdiction, and party autonomy.

The dispute originated from a development agreement, with the arbitral tribunal, comprising three former High Court judges, establishing a fee schedule from the outset. Marvel Sigma consistently failed to meet its obligations, accumulating a significant shortfall despite multiple reminders, conditional orders, and broken undertakings. Ultimately, after numerous extensions and no part-payment offered even at a final hearing, the tribunal concluded that the claimant lacked bona fides and was prejudicing the counterclaimants. It consequently terminated Marvel Sigma's claims, imposing Rs 10 lakh in costs, and directed the counterclaim to advance.

Marvel Sigma's writ petition argued that since the Arbitration Act does not provide an immediate statutory challenge to a Section 38(2) termination, a constitutional writ was the only available recourse. The petitioner relied on Supreme Court precedents, including Deep Industries Limited v. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited, where a writ was entertained for a Section 32(2)(c) termination, and Oil and Natural Gas Corporation v. Afcons Gunanusa JV, asserting that arbitrators cannot unilaterally impose fee regimes, emphasizing party autonomy. They further contended that the termination, despite substantial payments, violated principles of natural justice.

The respondents countered, asserting that a writ petition is only maintainable for jurisdictional error or gross injustice, neither of which was evident. They argued that Section 38(2), read with Sections 31(8) and 31A, expressly empowers the tribunal to dismiss parties failing to pay cost deposits. The fee schedule, they noted, was mutually agreed upon, and the petitioner had received ample opportunities, making the fault lie with the claimant's default, not the tribunal's order.

Justice Pitale analyzed three core questions: the maintainability of a writ against a Section 38(2) termination, whether the arbitrators exceeded jurisdiction or breached natural justice, and the applicability of the cited Supreme Court precedents. The Court acknowledged the Arbitration Act's "vacuum" regarding direct challenges to Section 38(2) terminations but concluded that this vacuum is not universally filled by writ jurisdiction. Instead, an aggrieved party could pursue an alternate remedy under Section 14 of the Act, which allows for the removal of an arbitrator or setting aside of an order if the mandate has terminated. The Court found no excess of jurisdiction, citing Section 31A and 31(8), which vest the tribunal with the power to fix and secure costs. Natural justice was also not violated, given the extensive opportunities granted to Marvel Sigma. Furthermore, the Court distinguished Afcons Gunanusa, as the fee structure in this case was agreed upon at the outset, unlike a unilateral imposition.

Ultimately, the Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition, finding that Marvel Sigma had failed to demonstrate a prima facie case of jurisdictional overreach or gross injustice. The judgment reinforces that arbitration, while a private dispute resolution mechanism, is not cost-free. Parties agreeing to fee schedules must adhere to them, as repeated defaults can lead to the dismissal of claims. The decision also subtly signals that writ courts will generally refrain from acting as appellate bodies when parallel statutory remedies, such as Section 14 of the Arbitration Act, are available.

title: Rajasthan High Court Orders FSSAI to Frame Regulations on Genetically Modified Foods, Citing Right to Safe Food under Article 21
description:
The Rajasthan High Court, in the case of Kritesh Oswal & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., has issued a significant directive compelling the Central Government and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to promptly frame and notify regulations for genetically modified (GM) foods under Section 22 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The Court emphasized that the current absence of such regulations constitutes a regulatory vacuum, posing substantial risks to public health and infringing upon the fundamental right to life and health guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution.

This ruling emerged from a Public Interest Litigation highlighting the unregulated sale, import, and distribution of GM food products in India, particularly edible oils like soybean and canola, without requisite scientific evaluation of their health impacts. Petitioners argued that despite the FSS Act mandating a framework, FSSAI had failed to establish regulations, allowing GM ingredients into the market without proper oversight or safety standards. The petition also challenged the legality of merely labelling GM products under existing rules without a fundamental regulatory approval process.

The Court underscored the State's affirmative duty under Article 47 to ensure safe nutrition, asserting that food security cannot undermine food safety. It invoked the precautionary principle, stressing that potential harm from unregulated GM foods necessitates robust oversight. Key findings included that the absence of regulations directly violates Article 21, that FSSAI is the sole competent authority for GM food regulation, and that consumers possess a fundamental right to know about GM ingredients in their food. The Court also deemed any prior approvals by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) for GM foods as illegal and non-binding.

Consequently, the Rajasthan High Court directed FSSAI to finalize and notify the GM food regulations within three months. Furthermore, it mandated that no GM food product, whether raw, processed, or as an ingredient, should be imported, manufactured, or sold in India without FSSAI approval and compliance with the new regulations, including specific labelling requirements. The judgment reinforces that food safety is a constitutional imperative deeply connected to human dignity, urging proactive governance to align scientific advancement with public welfare and constitutional values.

title: Housewife-Landlady’s Right to Seek Eviction for Husband’s Welfare: Delhi High Court Upholds Bona-Fide Requirement under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act
description:
The Delhi High Court, in the case of Naveen Kumar v. Babita Jain, has issued a significant ruling affirming that a housewife who owns a tenanted property can legitimately seek eviction of a tenant if the premises are required for her husband's welfare or to enable him to start a business. This decision clarifies that familial obligations and spousal dependence fall within the ambit of "for his own use" as defined under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, emphasizing the gender-neutral application of rent control laws.

The dispute arose when Mrs. Babita Jain, the landlady and a housewife, filed an eviction petition seeking possession of a tenanted shop for her husband to commence a dry-fruits business. The Additional Rent Controller granted the eviction, prompting the tenant to appeal to the Delhi High Court. The tenant argued that the landlady, as a housewife without an independent income, could not claim eviction for her husband's benefit and that the asserted need was fabricated.

The High Court rejected the tenant's contentions, affirming that gender or occupation is immaterial in determining a bona-fide need. Citing the Supreme Court's judgment in Joginder Pal v. Naval Kishore Behal, the Court reiterated that "for his own use" must be interpreted liberally to include dependent family members. It held that a housewife possesses equal rights to seek eviction for the welfare or livelihood of her dependents, and to interpret the statute otherwise would amount to discrimination, violating Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. The Court found the landlady's claim genuine, noting the tenant's failure to provide evidence disproving the need or showing the husband's alternative employment.

Ultimately, the Court upheld the Additional Rent Controller's finding that the landlady's need for the premises for her husband's business was genuine and bona fide. It dismissed the tenant's revision petition and recorded the tenant's undertaking to vacate the premises by May 30, 2026. This judgment underscores that familial welfare and economic dignity are central to the concept of bona-fide requirement, harmonizing the Delhi Rent Control Act with constitutional principles of gender neutrality and reinforcing that ownership rights and legal entitlements are independent of economic participation or employment status.

title: Bombay High Court Reiterates: Borrowers Cannot Demand One-Time Settlement as a Matter of Right
description:
In a significant ruling, the Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench) in Ms. Archana Wani v. Indian Bank & Ors. affirmed that borrowers or guarantors do not possess a right to demand a One-Time Settlement (OTS), nor can courts compel banks to disclose internal settlement benchmarks or accept settlement proposals. The Court emphasized that loan recovery and settlement decisions fall squarely within the commercial wisdom of banks, which manage public funds and are bound by financial discipline. Judicial intervention under Article 226 of the Constitution is unwarranted, particularly when statutory remedies under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC), are available.

The case involved Ms. Archana Wani, a guarantor for a defaulted loan of ₹62 crore, whose account was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). After the bank initiated recovery proceedings under SARFAESI and IBC, Ms. Wani submitted multiple OTS proposals. These were rejected by the bank for not meeting its "benchmark criteria," which the petitioner argued were arbitrarily withheld. She sought judicial intervention to compel the bank to disclose its standards and accept her proposal.

The High Court meticulously reviewed the contractual obligations and statutory frameworks, concluding that a bank's decision on an OTS proposal is a purely commercial one based on internal policies and risk assessment. The Court reiterated that an OTS proposal does not confer any enforceable right upon the borrower, and banks are not statutorily obligated to disclose their internal benchmark parameters. Relying on established Supreme Court precedents, the Bench highlighted that compelling banks to settle on terms dictated by borrowers would undermine financial prudence and public interest. Consequently, the High Court dismissed the petition, reiterating that OTS schemes are discretionary concessions, not enforceable rights, and that negotiation, not entitlement, is the pathway to settlement. The interim stay on recovery was, however, continued for six weeks to allow the petitioner to explore alternate remedies.

title: Arms Act, 1959: Renewal is the Norm, Refusal the Exception, Rules Madras High Court
description:
The Madras High Court, in a significant ruling by its Madurai Bench, has clarified that while possessing a firearm is a regulated privilege under the Arms Act, 1959, the renewal of an existing licence, especially after peaceful use, should be considered the norm. Refusal of renewal, the Court asserted, must be based on explicit, rational, and case-specific findings, shifting the burden from the applicant to the licensing authority to provide compelling reasons.

This judgment arose from a petition filed by Magudapathi, an ordinary citizen who held a smooth bore gun licence since 2021 for crop protection and sport, which had been routinely renewed once. His application for a second renewal in 2024 was denied by the District Magistrate cum District Collector, Dindigul, solely on the grounds that Magudapathi was facing prosecution under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code for a fatal motor vehicle accident. The Collector deemed this a threat to "public safety," prompting Magudapathi to challenge the decision in the High Court.

Justice G.R. Swaminathan, examining Sections 13, 14, and 15 of the Arms Act, 1959, highlighted Section 15(3), which mandates that a licence "shall, unless the licensing authority for reasons to be recorded in writing otherwise decides, be renewable." The Court emphasized that this provision converts the initial privilege into an expectancy of renewal, which can only be defeated by reasons that meet the standards of Section 14, pertaining to refusal. The High Court found the Collector's justification "woefully insufficient," stating that a prosecution for negligent driving (Section 304A IPC) is distinct from firearm-related misconduct, nor does it indicate an individual is of unsound mind or unfit as per Section 14. Furthermore, the Court reiterated that while alternative remedies exist, it can intervene via writ jurisdiction when an impugned order is patently illegal.

Consequently, the High Court quashed the Collector's order and directed the renewal of Magudapathi’s gun licence for five years, subject to standard conditions. This ruling serves as a crucial reminder that administrative discretion in weapon licensing tightens once a citizen has demonstrated trustworthy conduct, safeguarding individual expectation and ensuring a principled application of the Arms Act against arbitrary denials based on unrelated criminal proceedings.

title: Statutory Stop-Watch Re-Set: Section 17(5) SARFAESI Act Comes Alive
description:
The Supreme Court, in the case of Indian Overseas Bank v. M/s Radhey Infra Solutions (Pvt.) Ltd., addressed the issue of delays in debt recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act. The court emphasized that the statutory timelines mandated by Section 17(5) of the Act must be strictly adhered to by Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs).

The case arose from a borrower's application under Section 17(1) of the SARFAESI Act, which remained pending before the DRT, Dehradun, for an extended period without any extension orders or recorded reasons. The Supreme Court underscored that Section 17(5) requires DRTs to dispose of such applications within 60 days, extendable by a maximum of four months with written justification for each extension. The Court criticized the High Court's previous order for not enforcing the timeline.

The Supreme Court directed the DRT, Dehradun, to immediately comply with Section 17(5) of the SARFAESI Act and dispose of the pending application expeditiously. This ruling serves as a reminder to all DRTs that the statutory timelines are not merely suggestive but are crucial for ensuring timely debt recovery and adjudication of borrower grievances, thereby reinforcing the importance of time in commercial matters.

title: Delhi High Court on Mental Cruelty: False Allegations, Vexatious Litigation and the Boundaries of Matrimonial Conduct
description:
The Delhi High Court in X v. Y upheld a divorce decree based on mental cruelty, reaffirming the definition of cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The court dismissed the wife's appeal, emphasizing that a consistent pattern of false allegations, unsubstantiated criminal complaints, and vindictive litigation constitutes sufficient grounds for divorce due to the mental anguish inflicted on the other spouse.

The case involved a marriage marred by extensive litigation, with the wife initiating numerous complaints, including those under Section 498A of the IPC and the Domestic Violence Act, most of which were later found to be baseless. The Family Court initially granted the divorce, citing the severe mental agony and social humiliation suffered by the husband due to the wife's actions.

The High Court's decision highlighted that mental cruelty encompasses not only physical harm but also emotional distress caused by repeated baseless accusations, character assassination, and the misuse of legal provisions. While "irretrievable breakdown of marriage" is not a statutory ground for divorce, the court acknowledged that prolonged separation and loss of trust, in conjunction with demonstrated cruelty, support the dissolution of marriage. The judgment serves as a significant precedent, urging courts to recognize the psychological impact of relentless litigation and ensuring that legal remedies are not weaponized for personal vendettas within matrimonial disputes.

title: Supreme Court Addresses Conflict Between Forest Rights Act and Forest Conservation Act on Tribal Housing
description:
In Sugra Adiwasi & Ors. v. Pathranand & Ors., the Supreme Court of India examined the intersection of the Forest Rights Act (FRA) and the Forest Conservation Act (FCA) concerning the construction of permanent housing for forest dwellers. The court acknowledged the conflict between recognizing the rights of tribal communities to adequate housing and the need to preserve forest ecology.

The case arose from a dispute over whether forest dwellers could construct permanent homes on forest land without violating the FCA. Petitioners argued the FRA grants habitation rights, including durable housing, while the Union of India emphasized the FCA's role in forest preservation. The core legal issue was whether FRA-recognized construction could proceed despite FCA regulations.

The Court analyzed both Acts, noting the FRA's limited "notwithstanding" clause doesn't explicitly authorize housing construction without FCA oversight. It reaffirmed that the FCA regulates, rather than prohibits, non-forest activities, emphasizing forest protection as a constitutional obligation. The court stressed the need for a "convergent interpretation" where both statutes coexist, protecting human and environmental interests.

Acknowledging the State's duty to ensure minimum living conditions, the Supreme Court directed the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to formulate a regulatory mechanism enabling dwelling construction for forest dwellers, ensuring FCA compliance. This directive emphasizes inter-departmental coordination and a balanced approach, reflecting a commitment to both social justice and environmental stewardship.

title: Supreme Court Clarifies Limitation and Validity of Arbitration Clauses Post-Amendment
description:
In Offshore Infrastructures Ltd. v. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd., the Supreme Court of India addressed the validity of arbitration clauses impacted by statutory amendments and the computation of limitation for applications seeking arbitrator appointments under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The ruling underscores the pro-arbitration stance of Indian courts and provides clarity on interpreting arbitration clauses in light of the 2015 Amendment.

The dispute stemmed from a contract between Offshore Infrastructures and Bharat Petroleum, where Offshore Infrastructures sought arbitration due to outstanding dues. The original arbitration clause designated the Managing Director of Bharat Petroleum as the sole arbitrator, a provision rendered inconsistent with the 2015 Amendment to the Arbitration Act, which aims to ensure arbitrator neutrality. The High Court dismissed Offshore Infrastructures' application for arbitrator appointment as time-barred, calculating the limitation period from the date of the No Claim Certificate.

The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, holding that the ineligibility of a named arbitrator does not invalidate the entire arbitration clause. It affirmed that the parties' intent to arbitrate remains valid and that courts retain the power under Section 11(6) to appoint an independent arbitrator. The Court further clarified the limitation period, considering the Supreme Court’s COVID-19-related extension orders. It ruled that the application was within the prescribed limitation period when accounting for the exclusion of time between March 15, 2020, and February 28, 2022.

The Supreme Court directed the matter to the Delhi International Arbitration Centre (DIAC) for the appointment of an independent arbitrator. This decision reinforces the principles of party autonomy, fairness, and the legislative intent behind the 2015 amendment, ensuring that technicalities do not undermine the fundamental goal of alternative dispute resolution.

title: Husband Cannot Use Child as a Pawn to Prove Wife’s Adultery – DNA Test Plea Dismissed
description:
The Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court dismissed a husband's petition seeking a DNA test on his child to prove his estranged wife's alleged adultery. The court emphasized the importance of protecting the child's rights, privacy, and dignity, reinforcing constitutional safeguards under Articles 20(3) and 21. The ruling highlights that DNA testing should not be used intrusively in litigation without strong justification.

The case arose from a maintenance petition filed by the wife after a divorce. The husband sought a DNA test, claiming his ex-wife had previously admitted the child was not his. The court ruled against this, citing the lack of a prima facie case, an inordinate delay since the divorce, and the potential harm to the child. The court referenced Section 116 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which presumes a child's legitimacy unless non-access is proven, a legal safeguard.

Justice Shamim Ahmed underscored that forensic methods should not infringe upon fundamental rights or be misused. The court stated that ordering a DNA test in this situation would violate the child's right to privacy and potentially cause lifelong stigma. The court concluded that the husband’s plea lacked merit and appeared to be an attempt to humiliate the wife and prolong the litigation. The judgment reaffirms the judiciary's commitment to the best interests of the child, privacy, and human dignity, preventing the weaponization of technology for emotional harm in family disputes.

title: Minors’ Rights Protected – Court Rules Suit Not Mandatory to Undo Guardian’s Unauthorized Sale
description:
The Supreme Court of India, in K.S. Shivappa v. Smt. K. Neelamma, clarified that a minor's repudiation of an unauthorized property sale by their guardian, without prior court permission under Section 8(2) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, does not necessarily require a formal lawsuit. Such a sale is voidable, not void, and repudiation can be effectively demonstrated through clear and unequivocal conduct, such as the subsequent sale of the property after attaining majority.

The case involved a dispute over land originally purchased in the names of three minor sons and later sold by their father/guardian without the required court permission. After attaining majority, the sons sold the land to a different party, thus repudiating the original sale. The Supreme Court examined the legal implications of Section 8(2) and 8(3) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 and ultimately ruled in favor of the sons' right to repudiate the sale through their conduct, emphasizing that the Act does not explicitly mandate a civil suit for setting aside such transactions.

The Court underscored that once a voidable transaction is avoided by the minor, it becomes void ab initio. The Supreme Court's decision highlights the importance of protecting minors' property rights while promoting fairness and clarity in property law and strengthens both substantive justice and transactional integrity.

title: Kerala's Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025: A Step Towards Work-Life Balance
description:
The Kerala Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025, introduced by Dr. N. Jayaraj, aims to address the blurring lines between work and personal life due to hyper-connectivity. This private member's bill seeks to legally recognize an employee's right to disconnect from work-related communications after hours, mirroring similar initiatives in European countries.

The bill arises from increasing employee burnout and the "always-on" work culture, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. It aims to provide statutory protections, ensuring employees can disengage without fear of retaliation. Key provisions include defining the "Right to Disconnect," prohibiting punitive actions against employees who exercise this right, establishing grievance redressal committees, and enabling the Labour Commissioner to enforce compliance.

The bill aligns with the Indian Constitution, particularly Article 21, which guarantees the right to life with dignity, and Articles 38, 39, and 43, which mandate humane working conditions. It addresses the statutory gap in existing labor laws concerning digital extension of labor beyond physical working hours. While facing challenges in enforceability and requiring consideration for sectoral flexibility, the bill catalyzes crucial discussions on redefining workplace rights in the digital age.

title: Patna High Court Balances Discipline and Reform in Student Impersonation Case
description:
The Patna High Court, in Bhawesh Kumar Bhaskar v. State of Bihar & Others, delivered a significant judgment addressing the proportionality of punishment for medical students accused of impersonation. The court examined whether permanent expulsion was an appropriate disciplinary action, balancing the need for academic integrity with constitutional principles of fairness and the right to life and dignity.

The case involved five MBBS students accused of impersonation during examinations. The University's Unfair Means Committee recommended their expulsion, which the Vice Chancellor approved. The students argued that permanent expulsion was excessively harsh and violated their fundamental rights, especially considering the discretionary powers available to the Vice Chancellor under the University Statute. They referenced precedents emphasizing proportionality in punishment and advocating for a reformative approach to discipline.

The University defended its decision, citing the severity of impersonation and the need to maintain academic credibility. They argued that the "Rules for Unfair Means" were properly implemented and that students were bound by the University's disciplinary jurisdiction.

The High Court held that while it respects academic autonomy, it can intervene in cases of arbitrary or disproportionate punishment. Justice Sinha found that the Vice Chancellor had mechanically accepted the Committee's recommendation without independent reasoning. The Court emphasized that permanent expulsion was excessively harsh for first-time offenders, preventing any chance of reform. Consequently, the court modified the punishments, emphasizing that this leniency should not be mistaken for condoning the misconduct. The decision serves as a precedent for balancing discipline and empathy in educational institutions to shape responsible citizens.

title: Delhi High Court Clarifies: Delhi Government Can Regulate Private School Fees Only to Prevent Profiteering, Not to Control Fee Structure
description:
The Delhi High Court, in a ruling on LPA 213/2024, LPA 316/2024, and LPA 669/2024, affirmed that the Directorate of Education (DoE) of Delhi's power to regulate fees charged by recognized unaided private schools is limited. The Court clarified that this regulation can only be exercised to prevent profiteering, commercialization, or capitation fees, ensuring that collected fees are exclusively used for educational purposes, as mandated by the Delhi School Education Act, 1973 (DSEA) and the Delhi School Education Rules, 1973 (DSER).

The judgment, delivered by a Division Bench, reaffirms the autonomy of private unaided institutions while protecting against exploitation. The case originated from writ petitions by Bluebells School International and Lilawati Vidya Mandir Senior Secondary School, challenging DoE orders restricting fee increases. A Single Judge previously quashed the orders, permitting DoE to act only against profiteering.

The central legal issue was whether the DoE could control the fee structure or if its power was confined to preventing profiteering. The Court analyzed Sections 17, 18, and 24 of the DSEA and Rules 172-177 of the DSER, noting the statutory framework promotes transparency but doesn't empower DoE to dictate fee structures. The Court referenced precedents like T.M.A. Pai Foundation and Modern School v. Union of India, emphasizing the state's duty to prevent exploitation but not to micromanage finances.

The High Court upheld that the DoE may regulate fees only to prevent profiteering, ensuring funds are used for educational purposes. While the court dismissed the appeals and affirmed the Single Judge's judgment, it granted the DoE the liberty to proceed against the schools if statutory violations are found, provided due procedure and natural justice are followed. This decision balances autonomy and accountability, empowering the State to prevent abuse while protecting institutional autonomy.

title: SEBI's AI/ML Reporting Framework: Evolution and Harmonisation Across Indian Stock Exchanges
description:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) introduced a structured reporting framework in 2019 to oversee the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies in India's securities markets. This framework aims to balance technological innovation with regulatory oversight, ensuring transparency, auditability, and accountability in algorithmic trading and intermediary functions. The initiative is part of SEBI's broader Enhanced Supervision Programme, designed to strengthen technology governance and systemic risk management.

Initially, SEBI directed all recognised exchanges to establish a uniform supervisory framework for tracking AI/ML systems used by intermediaries. The Metropolitan Stock Exchange (MSE) implemented this through half-yearly reporting obligations, requiring members to disclose details of AI/ML systems used for trading, risk management, or investor servicing, even mandating NIL declarations for those not using such systems. In 2023, the reporting framework was broadened to include predictive, analytical, and pattern-recognition algorithms used across various functions, with greater emphasis on auditability and documentation.

In 2025, the National Stock Exchange (NSE) introduced a cross-exchange reporting mechanism, allowing trading members registered with NSE to make a single AI/ML disclosure filing shared with other exchanges. This harmonised model, adopted by MSE, reduces duplication and simplifies compliance for multi-exchange firms. The framework mandates that all algorithmic trading members report the use of AI/ML systems, whether developed in-house or procured from third-party vendors, and maintain comprehensive documentation for supervisory reviews. SEBI's approach emphasizes technological neutrality with regulatory accountability, ensuring that AI/ML tools operate within parameters that protect market integrity and investor trust.

title: Reliance Industries Secures Injunction Against “Jiocabs.com” for Trademark Infringement
description:
Reliance Industries Limited, owner of the registered "JIO" trademark, filed a commercial intellectual property suit against Asif Ahmed, registrant of the domain www.jiocabs.com, and Usman, proprietor of Doon Taxi Service, alleging trademark and copyright infringement. Reliance asserted that the defendants were operating taxi services under the "JIO" name, utilizing deceptively similar logos and artwork, thereby passing off their services as associated with Reliance's well-known brand. The suit sought a permanent injunction, restraining the defendants from infringing the trademark, passing off goods and services, and using the domain name or similar artwork, along with a request to suspend and transfer the domain name.

The court considered evidence including trademark registrations, side-by-side comparisons of the marks, and WhatsApp transcripts demonstrating the defendants' active use of the "JIO" name for taxi operations. The court also noted that the defendants altered their business name and website content after receiving a legal notice, which the court interpreted as an implicit acknowledgement of the infringement. Reliance further presented precedents recognizing "JIO" as a well-known trademark, reinforcing their claim.

The court granted an ad-interim injunction restraining the defendants from using the domain name www.jiocabs.com, the "JIO" mark, or any deceptively similar mark in relation to taxi services, as well as prohibiting the use of similar artwork. The court found that Reliance established trademark infringement and passing off, with the balance of convenience favoring the plaintiff, who would suffer irreparable injury without the injunction. The defendants were granted the opportunity to apply for variation or vacation of the order, and the matter was scheduled for further consideration of interim relief at a later date.

title: Fake Licence Not Enough to Deny Insurance: Supreme Court
description:
The Supreme Court of India, in Hind Samachar Ltd. (Delhi Unit) v. National Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors., has clarified that a vehicle owner cannot be held liable solely based on the subsequent discovery of a fake driver's license. The court emphasized that an insurer must demonstrate a deliberate violation of policy conditions or substantial evidence of collusion to deny indemnification. This decision bolsters the legal framework surrounding "pay and recover" cases under the Motor Vehicles Act, reinforcing the principle that an insured owner's good faith is presumed unless proven otherwise.

The case stemmed from a fatal road accident involving a truck owned by Hind Samachar Ltd. and a Matador van. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) initially ruled both vehicles negligent and directed the truck's insurer to indemnify the owner, despite allegations of a fake driver's license. The Delhi High Court reversed this, finding collusion and granting the insurer the right to recover compensation from the owner.

The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, emphasizing that the insurer failed to provide sufficient evidence of collusion or negligence on the owner's part. The court reiterated that the insurer bears the burden of proving the insured knowingly entrusted the vehicle to an unqualified driver or willfully breached policy conditions. The court found that the owner acted with reasonable diligence by verifying the driver's license and producing renewal records from the licensing authority.

The Supreme Court concluded that without proof of willful breach or collusion, the High Court's direction allowing the insurer to recover compensation from the vehicle owner was legally unsound. The ruling reaffirms that vehicle owners are not expected to conduct exhaustive license verification unless there are specific reasons for suspicion. The decision reinforces the welfare intent of the Motor Vehicles Act to ensure victim compensation without unjustly burdening owners acting in good faith.

title: Food Safety or Competition Issue? CCI Draws the Line in Maggi Sauce Case
description:
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) dismissed a complaint against Nestle India Limited concerning alleged use of contaminated water in the production of Maggi Sauce at its Goa factory. The complaint, filed by Sarvesh M. Kolumbkar, accused Nestle of violating the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and abusing its dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act. The informant sought an investigation into a purported "Maggi Sauce scam" and requested interim relief.

The CCI found no prima facie contravention of the Competition Act, clarifying that the allegations centered on food safety, hygiene, and product labelling, issues under the jurisdiction of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). The Commission emphasized that the alleged use of dirty water and mislabelling did not constitute anti-competitive practices or demonstrate that Nestle exploited its market position to restrict competitors or harm consumers.

The decision reinforces that unethical business practices do not automatically equate to abuse of dominance unless they directly impact market competition. The CCI underscored its role in ensuring market fairness and efficiency, distinct from addressing general consumer grievances or regulatory non-compliance related to food safety. The order clarifies the boundary between competition law and sectoral regulation, directing concerns regarding public health, product contamination, or deceptive labelling to appropriate authorities like the FSSAI.

title: Arbitral Award Must Be Within the Parameters of the Agreement Between the Parties
description:
Arbitration is rooted in party autonomy, where consent forms the basis of the tribunal's jurisdiction, scope, and authority. An arbitral award must adhere to the contract's parameters; deviations, either by disregarding terms or granting inconsistent relief, undermine the agreement's sanctity and the tribunal's jurisdiction, making the award vulnerable under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

The Indian arbitration framework, particularly Section 28(3) of the Act, emphasizes contractual sanctity, mandating tribunals to decide per the contract's terms. Arbitrators interpret, but do not rewrite, contracts based on equity or fairness. The Supreme Court of India has consistently reinforced that tribunals are creations of the contract, unable to exceed their mandate. Awards violating express terms are deemed patently illegal and against public policy.

Evidentiary discipline and procedural adherence are crucial, especially concerning contractual preconditions like notices or written approvals. Tribunals cannot waive these stipulations unless permitted by the contract. The Supreme Court has reinforced that commercial fairness cannot override contractual discipline, as seen in SEPCO Electric Power Construction Corporation vs. GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd., where the court set aside a tribunal's decision for wrongly invoking equitable estoppel to overlook mandatory contractual notices.

Judicial review under Sections 34 and 37 serves as a safeguard against arbitral excess, intervening when awards exhibit patent illegality or violate public policy, ensuring arbitration remains true to party consent. Contracting parties must draft precisely and adhere to performance requirements. Courts assess whether awards respect the agreement's boundaries, exercising restraint when faithful interpretations exist and correcting departures.

Arbitration's strength lies in predictability and respect for autonomy. Tribunals upholding the agreement's integrity reinforce commercial certainty. Conversely, exceeding mandates undermines the process. Awards must be rooted in the contract, ensuring arbitration remains an extension of party autonomy governed by the rule of contract.

title: CCI Dismisses Allegations Against BSNL: Tender Disqualification Not Anti-Competitive
description:
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) addressed a case filed by M/s C.C.L. Optoelectronics Private Ltd. against Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. (BSNL), alleging abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002. The informant contested BSNL's disqualification of its bid for a tender concerning Splice Closures for Optical Fiber Cables, arguing that the tender conditions were discriminatory and favored certain bidders.

The CCI, upon examination, defined the relevant market as Telecommunication Services in India. It found that BSNL's market share (approximately 2.09%) was significantly smaller than those of its major competitors, such as Reliance Jio, Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea. The commission concluded that BSNL did not hold a dominant position. It also noted that the disqualification was based on past performance criteria, not turnover.

Ultimately, the CCI determined that no prima facie case of contravention of Section 4 of the Act was established against BSNL. The Commission closed the matter under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act, 2002, dismissing the application for interim relief and concluding that BSNL's actions did not constitute abuse of dominance or restrictive trade practices.

title: RBI's Draft Directions on Lending to Related Parties: A Summary
description:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has released the Draft Reserve Bank of India (Lending to Related Parties) Directions, 2025, seeking public input by October 31, 2025. This draft aims to establish a unified, principle-based framework for transactions between regulated entities (REs) and their related parties, an area of long-standing concern regarding governance and prudential oversight.

Currently, regulations on lending to related parties are fragmented across various regulatory frameworks, leading to potential arbitrage and ambiguity. The new draft directions intend to harmonize governance standards, enhance transparency in related-party exposures, and strengthen market discipline across all REs, including banks, NBFCs, and cooperative banks.

Key provisions include a broad definition of "related parties" aligned with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS 24), materiality-based thresholds for Board or committee approval of transactions, and a principle-based exemption to Section 20(1)(b) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The draft also mandates comprehensive reporting and disclosure obligations to align with international best practices.

The proposed framework emphasizes ethical governance and conflict of interest management, requiring financial institutions to embed robust governance and risk management practices. Non-compliance may lead to regulatory action and reputational consequences. This initiative, part of broader reforms promoting uniformity and sound corporate governance, follows the Final Co-Lending Framework. The RBI invites stakeholder feedback before finalizing the directions, which will supersede existing circulars.

Ultimately, the Draft Lending to Related Parties Directions, 2025, represent a crucial step toward promoting integrity, transparency, and uniform governance in India's financial system, balancing operational flexibility with prudential discipline to enhance resilience and credibility.

title: Bombay High Court Upholds Mother’s Right To Custody After Father’s Death
description:
The Bombay High Court, Aurangabad Bench, in Parvati Swati v. Vyankat & Anr., reaffirmed a mother's right to custody following the father's death, emphasizing the paramount importance of the child's welfare under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. The ruling underscores that while grandparents can provide love, the mother, as the natural guardian, holds the inherent right and responsibility unless proven unfit.

The case arose after the father's death, where the paternal grandparents sought guardianship of the minor child, whose custody had been granted to the father in a prior divorce decree. The mother filed a counter-application seeking custody, which was initially rejected. The High Court addressed whether the grandparents could claim custody in preference to the mother, citing Section 6(a) of the Act, which favors the mother as the natural guardian after the father's death, especially for children below five.

The Court considered arguments from both sides, including the mother's improved financial stability and the child's established relationship with the grandparents. Justice Chapalgaonkar, reiterating the child's welfare as paramount, ruled in favor of the mother, citing precedents that a natural parent's custody should only be denied if they are demonstrably unfit. The Court granted custody to the mother while providing visitation rights to the grandparents, balancing the child's legal right to maternal care with the importance of maintaining family bonds. This judgment reaffirms the principle that a mother's care is irreplaceable while emphasizing the need for compassion and justice in guardianship law.

title: Music Legend Asha Bhosle Sues AI Firm and E-Commerce Sites Over Voice and Image Misuse
description:
The Bombay High Court has granted ad-interim protection to playback singer Asha Bhosle, recognizing her personality rights against unauthorized use of her voice, image, and likeness by AI platforms and online marketplaces. This ruling sets a precedent in India's jurisprudence on deepfakes, AI exploitation, and publicity rights by acknowledging the legal protection of a celebrity's persona, extending to voice cloning, AI-generated content, and digital merchandise.

The case arose from the misappropriation of Asha Bhosle's voice, name, image, and likeness without her consent. AI platforms were developing tools to clone her voice, allowing users to generate songs in her style, which were then circulated on platforms like YouTube. Additionally, online marketplaces like Amazon and Flipkart were selling unauthorized merchandise featuring her image. Bhosle argued these actions violated her personality rights and moral rights under Section 38-B of the Copyright Act, 1957.

The Bombay High Court concluded that Bhosle had established a strong prima facie case, emphasizing the unauthorized technological exploitation of her identity and reputation. The court issued ad-interim injunctions, restraining the defendants from misusing her personality attributes.

This judgment significantly shapes India's response to AI, deepfakes, and personality rights. It affirms that a celebrity's voice, name, and likeness are protectable attributes, and AI voice cloning without consent constitutes infringement. The ruling also places a duty on intermediaries like Amazon, Flipkart, and YouTube to remove infringing content and share violator details, strengthening accountability in the digital ecosystem. While this judgment provides immediate relief, it also exposes the regulatory vacuum in India regarding AI-generated content and digital impersonation, highlighting the need for comprehensive legislation on digital identity and AI misuse.

title: Project Financing in India: A Comprehensive Overview
description:
Project financing is a critical mechanism for funding large-scale infrastructure and industrial projects in India, relying on projected cash flows rather than sponsor balance sheets. It has become increasingly important for India's economic growth as the country develops essential infrastructure. The project financing ecosystem in India consists of equity, debt, and government support mechanisms and is underpinned by both public and private sector investment, as well as growing institutional support.

Project finance is widely used across multiple infrastructure sectors in India. However, despite its growth, this ecosystem faces several persistent and emerging challenges, including those related to the legal and regulatory framework.

Recent trends emphasize the need to strengthen project preparation, enhance risk-sharing mechanisms, deepen bond markets, promote dispute resolution reforms, and leverage innovative financing tools like InvITs, ESG bonds, and blended finance. As India aims for a $5 trillion economy, robust project finance mechanisms will be vital for mobilizing the necessary capital for sustainable infrastructure development.

title: Delhi High Court on Currency Accessibility: Relief for Visually Impaired Persons
description:
The Delhi High Court addressed petitions concerning the difficulties visually impaired individuals face in identifying Indian currency notes, particularly the ₹50 denomination introduced post-demonetization. The court emphasized that accessibility is a constitutional and statutory mandate under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act), requiring the State to ensure equal access to financial infrastructure.

The petitions arose after the 2016 demonetization, as the reduced size variations in the new Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series notes made tactile identification challenging. The court formed a High-Powered Committee, led by Prof. M. Balakrishnan of IIT Delhi, to investigate and provide recommendations.
